Whole House Filters Whole house water filter systems are devices that customers can buy privately to treat their water. Issues to Keep in Mind Bacteria — Most water filters must be changed every 30 days to prevent bacteria from growing, and many water filters eliminate chlorine. The town adds chlorine to its drinking water for disinfection. Without adequate disinfection, bacteria will start to grow. Poor Water Quality — Use of a filter that eliminates chlorine will cause free ammonia to be left in the filtered water. This could cause chemical substances in the water to change, resulting in poor water quality. Specifically, ammonium salts could change to nitrites and then nitrates in a process called nitrification. Nitrate contamination can be unhealthy, particularly for infants. Hillsborough adds ammonia to water as part of its disinfection process. The ammonia bonds with chlorine to produce chloramines to cleanse water. Water Testing — If a water quality issue occurs in a home with a whole house filter system, the town cannot test the water. Whole house filters provide secondary treatment to water. Test results at homes with these filters would not provide data on the water that Hillsborough delivers.

Hillsborough's treated wastewater is released into the Eno River. Before the water is safe to return to the river, it must go through multiple stages of treatment at the Wastewater Treatment Plant. The Eno River is within the Upper Neuse River Basin, an ecologically sensitive area. Due to this, the state imposes strict requirements on treated wastewater. Staff who maintain the pipes and pumps connected with removing your used water must be available at all hours for emergencies. The Upper Neuse River Watershed is the 770-square-mile area draining to the Falls Lake Reservoir. Our Watershed Falls Lake Rules Hillsborough is required to treat its wastewater at higher and more expensive standards than other sewer systems because it is in a watershed that drains into Falls Lake. The lake is a 12,000-acre reservoir in Durham, Granville and Wake counties. It is on the Environmental Protection Agency’s list of impaired waters and has been designated nutrient-sensitive by the North Carolina Division of Water Resources. To protect and restore the lake’s water quality, the state created the Falls Lake Rules to reduce the amount of nitrogen and phosphorous that enter Falls Lake through rivers and streams. The first stage of the wastewater discharge rules went into effect in 2016, and the second stage is expected in 2036. In 2014, Hillsborough completed upgrades to its wastewater treatment plant in part to meet the Stage 1 wastewater rule. Additional upgrades to the Wastewater Treatment Plant likely will be required to meet the Stage 2 wastewater rules. Read more about the rules from the Upper Neuse River Basin Association . Nitrogen and Phosphorus Removal Hillsborough's wastewater treatment work helps protect the Eno River, which is classified as nutrient sensitive. The town is dedicated to maintaining the high water quality of our river and has successfully reduced the total nitrogen discharged into the river by approximately 85% since 2004. In 2022, the town discharged into the Eno River only 57.6% of the allowed total nitrogen and 56.7% of the allowed total phosphorus. The allowances are provided by the Falls Lake Rules. Wastewater Treatment Our Treated Wastewater Quality The town's wastewater treatment must meet extremely high standards set by the town, state and federal governments. Hillsborough routinely tests for more than 220 substances in the town's wastewater and solids and meets or exceeds the standards. See the annual Wastewater Quality Report . Testing Staff monitor and evaluate water 24 hours a day. The plant has a laboratory to perform frequent checks on the progress of wastewater treatment. Staff also test various points in the Eno River.  Tests occur: Upstream of the water intake Before and after wastewater discharge Downstream of wastewater discharge Our Wastewater Treatment Process The plant uses an enhanced biological nutrient removal process to treat wastewater. Naturally occurring nutrients can cause algae growth, depleted oxygen, and fish kills. The nutrients — like nitrogen and phosphorus — must be brought to safe levels before treated wastewater can be discharged into the Eno River. Treatment Steps The Town of Hillsborough's wastewater treatment plant Large item removal — Bar screens remove trash, wood and rocks, which then are compacted for disposal. Grit removal — Sand and dirt are removed for disposal. Secondary treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are removed through a series of aeration tanks and sent to large tanks called digesters (see 4). The remaining wastewater moves to the clarifiers (see 5). Solids treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are treated in digesters and then thickened and trucked to a composting facility to be turned into a soil amendment. Clarification — Rakes slowly skim the wastewater surface for scum like grease, oils, plastics and soap. The scum is pumped to digesters (see 4). Solids settle and are removed for disposal. Sand filtration — The remaining water moves through 6 feet of sand, which removes additional solids. Disinfection, final treatment — Chlorine is added to kill bacteria. Chemicals are added to neutralize the chlorine. Aeration — The water is re-aerated before discharge to remove dissolved gases and to oxidize dissolved metals. Discharge — The treated wastewater is returned to the Eno River at an outfall. Wastewater Treatment Plant and Tours Wastewater Treatment Plant employees are highly certified and operate and maintain the plant to ensure compliance with state and federal permits and regulations. The plant can treat up to 3 million gallons of wastewater per day. It was built in 1977, with upgrades in 2001 and 2007 to improve solids management, nutrient removal and treatment capabilities. The most recent expansion and upgrade was completed in 2014, allowing the plant to meet state requirements to protect Falls Lake, where Hillsborough’s watershed drains. This upgrade Hillsborough’s discharged water quality among the best in the nation. Awards In previous years, the Wastewater Treatment Plant and its staff have won awards for: Professionalism in the Operation of a Wastewater Treatment Plant Solutions to Operational Problems Wastewater Treatment Plant Operations and Maintenance Wastewater Treatment Plant Operator Tours See what it takes to treat used water for return to the Eno River. Public tours are offered at 1 p.m. on the second Friday of the month in March and September. Private tours can be scheduled separately for special groups. All tours are open to a maximum of 10 people with participants at least 10 years old. All tours require a completed request form. Request a Tour Wastewater Collection and System Maintenance About Pump Stations A pump station is a collection chamber that uses pumps to lift wastewater from a lower elevation to a higher elevation, where the wastewater can flow by gravity. It pumps into a pressurized main called a force main, which ends in a sewer manhole. There, wastewater can flow by gravity to the Wastewater Treatment Plant. The pump stations require frequent maintenance and weekly inspections. Improperly disposed rags, wipes or other trash can cause expensive repairs. Failures can result in larger sanitary sewer overflows than from a gravity sewer, with subsequent fines from the state. Why Pump Stations? Hillsborough has more pump stations per customer than surrounding water and sewer systems because of the town's terrain. Also, the systems were likely preferred decades ago due to the low upfront costs. Some of the pump stations were built by developers and turned over to the town to own and operate. Blocked Sewer Lines The town assesses sewer blockages to determine the cause and location — whether they are on the utility or property owner's side of a sewer line. Customers may be responsible for the cost of investigation and repairs if their  actions cause a blockage in the town’s sewer main. Responsibilities The town owns and maintains the sewer main or sewer service line in public rights of ways or easements. It will clear blockages of lines in public rights of ways or easements. The town may require property owners to install or relocate cleanouts to the town's specifications. The town may agree to perform the work but may require reimbursement and the granting of property access from the customer. Property owners are responsible for blockages in the sewer service line between the house or structure on their property and the public right of way or easement. The town can require installation or relocation of a cleanout at the right of way or easement if one is not present. Sewer Cleanout A sewer cleanout is a capped pipe that allows access to the sewer line for maintenance and inspections. Cleanouts typically indicate the ownership line when located at the edge of the public right of way or easement. Sewer Maintenance The town’s primary responsibility for the sewer system is to protect the environment by maintaining unobstructed wastewater flow in the collection system’s main lines. Crews routinely do preventative maintenance and repairs, remove roots and clean sewer lines with pressure washers. Every year, staff is required by state mandate to hydraulically clean a minimum of 10% of the gravity sewer lines in the system. Smoke Testing Crews use non-toxic, non-staining vapor resembling smoke to identify leaks in the sewer system. During testing, it is normal to see smoke escaping from roof vents and from sinks or bathtubs that are not used frequently. If smoke appears from the sink or bathtub, try running water down the drain to fill the dry trap. If you see smoke indoors that is not due to a dry trap or that appears to be arising from the ground in your yard, call the Hillsborough Water Distribution and Collection Division at 919-296-9650 to have the problem investigated. The town will notify customers of private connection issues that require repair. The town will address issues with public sewer lines. For town and customers responsibilities, see the town Code of Ordinances, sections 14-21 and 14-22 . For more information, contact the utility maintenance supervisor at 919-296-9652. Wastewater Collection Division The Wastewater Collection Division cleans and repairs sewer lines and maintains sewage lift or pump stations. The town has: 100.82 miles of sewer lines, which includes: 84.06 miles of gravity sewer lines 16.76 miles of force main sewer lines 27 public pump stations 2,163 sewer manholes Awards In previous years, the Wastewater Collections Division and its staff have won awards from the N.C. American Water Works Association-Water Environment Association for: Outstanding Wastewater Collection Operator of the Year Small Wastewater Collection System of the Year Infrastructure Protection Fats, Oils and Grease Fats, oil and grease poured down the drain will collect and stick to plumbing and sewer lines. Over time, lines can become blocked, causing sewer backups or overflows. Properties that discharge greasy wastewater are required to have interceptors for fats, oil and grease. Residential customers can obtain a free fat trapper from the town. They also should: Discard used fats, oil and grease with other garbage or recycle at an Orange County solid waste convenience center. Avoid or limit use of garbage disposals. Scrape plates into trash cans. Use paper towels to wipe leftover oils and fats from pots and pans. Fat Trappers The town provides fat trappers to water and sewer customers to help keep grease and oils out of the sewer system. To receive a fat trapper or additional bags, contact the utilities infrastructure protection supervisor or visit the Town Hall Annex, 105 E. Corbin St., where water bills are paid. Video Fats, Oils and Grease Program No Wipes in the Pipes Only waste and toilet paper should be flushed. Household cleaning and personal hygiene products labeled as flushable or safe for sewer or septic systems do not dissolve. Additionally, do not dispose of trash, medicine or other items in the sewer system. These items clog sewer lines and can damage sewer pumps and other equipment. For more information, contact the utilities infrastructure protection supervisor. In 2014, Hillsborough completed upgrades to its wastewater treatment plant in part to meet the Stage 1 wastewater rule. Additional upgrades to the Wastewater Treatment Plant likely will be required to meet the Stage 2 wastewater rules.
Read more about the rules from the Upper Neuse River Basin Association .

Nitrogen and Phosphorus Removal Hillsborough's wastewater treatment work helps protect the Eno River, which is classified as nutrient sensitive. The town is dedicated to maintaining the high water quality of our river and has successfully reduced the total nitrogen discharged into the river by approximately 85% since 2004. In 2022, the town discharged into the Eno River only 57.6% of the allowed total nitrogen and 56.7% of the allowed total phosphorus. The allowances are provided by the Falls Lake Rules.

Our Treated Wastewater Quality The town's wastewater treatment must meet extremely high standards set by the town, state and federal governments. Hillsborough routinely tests for more than 220 substances in the town's wastewater and solids and meets or exceeds the standards. See the annual Wastewater Quality Report . Testing Staff monitor and evaluate water 24 hours a day. The plant has a laboratory to perform frequent checks on the progress of wastewater treatment. Staff also test various points in the Eno River.  Tests occur: Upstream of the water intake Before and after wastewater discharge Downstream of wastewater discharge Our Wastewater Treatment Process The plant uses an enhanced biological nutrient removal process to treat wastewater. Naturally occurring nutrients can cause algae growth, depleted oxygen, and fish kills. The nutrients — like nitrogen and phosphorus — must be brought to safe levels before treated wastewater can be discharged into the Eno River. Treatment Steps The Town of Hillsborough's wastewater treatment plant Large item removal — Bar screens remove trash, wood and rocks, which then are compacted for disposal. Grit removal — Sand and dirt are removed for disposal. Secondary treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are removed through a series of aeration tanks and sent to large tanks called digesters (see 4). The remaining wastewater moves to the clarifiers (see 5). Solids treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are treated in digesters and then thickened and trucked to a composting facility to be turned into a soil amendment. Clarification — Rakes slowly skim the wastewater surface for scum like grease, oils, plastics and soap. The scum is pumped to digesters (see 4). Solids settle and are removed for disposal. Sand filtration — The remaining water moves through 6 feet of sand, which removes additional solids. Disinfection, final treatment — Chlorine is added to kill bacteria. Chemicals are added to neutralize the chlorine. Aeration — The water is re-aerated before discharge to remove dissolved gases and to oxidize dissolved metals. Discharge — The treated wastewater is returned to the Eno River at an outfall. Wastewater Treatment Plant and Tours Wastewater Treatment Plant employees are highly certified and operate and maintain the plant to ensure compliance with state and federal permits and regulations. The plant can treat up to 3 million gallons of wastewater per day. It was built in 1977, with upgrades in 2001 and 2007 to improve solids management, nutrient removal and treatment capabilities. The most recent expansion and upgrade was completed in 2014, allowing the plant to meet state requirements to protect Falls Lake, where Hillsborough’s watershed drains. This upgrade Hillsborough’s discharged water quality among the best in the nation. About Pump Stations A pump station is a collection chamber that uses pumps to lift wastewater from a lower elevation to a higher elevation, where the wastewater can flow by gravity. It pumps into a pressurized main called a force main, which ends in a sewer manhole. There, wastewater can flow by gravity to the Wastewater Treatment Plant. The pump stations require frequent maintenance and weekly inspections. Improperly disposed rags, wipes or other trash can cause expensive repairs. Failures can result in larger sanitary sewer overflows than from a gravity sewer, with subsequent fines from the state. Why Pump Stations? Hillsborough has more pump stations per customer than surrounding water and sewer systems because of the town's terrain. Also, the systems were likely preferred decades ago due to the low upfront costs. Some of the pump stations were built by developers and turned over to the town to own and operate. Blocked Sewer Lines The town assesses sewer blockages to determine the cause and location — whether they are on the utility or property owner's side of a sewer line. Customers may be responsible for the cost of investigation and repairs if their  actions cause a blockage in the town’s sewer main. Responsibilities The town owns and maintains the sewer main or sewer service line in public rights of ways or easements. It will clear blockages of lines in public rights of ways or easements. The town may require property owners to install or relocate cleanouts to the town's specifications. The town may agree to perform the work but may require reimbursement and the granting of property access from the customer. Property owners are responsible for blockages in the sewer service line between the house or structure on their property and the public right of way or easement. The town can require installation or relocation of a cleanout at the right of way or easement if one is not present. Sewer Cleanout A sewer cleanout is a capped pipe that allows access to the sewer line for maintenance and inspections. Cleanouts typically indicate the ownership line when located at the edge of the public right of way or easement. Sewer Maintenance The town’s primary responsibility for the sewer system is to protect the environment by maintaining unobstructed wastewater flow in the collection system’s main lines. Crews routinely do preventative maintenance and repairs, remove roots and clean sewer lines with pressure washers. Every year, staff is required by state mandate to hydraulically clean a minimum of 10% of the gravity sewer lines in the system. Smoke Testing Crews use non-toxic, non-staining vapor resembling smoke to identify leaks in the sewer system. During testing, it is normal to see smoke escaping from roof vents and from sinks or bathtubs that are not used frequently. If smoke appears from the sink or bathtub, try running water down the drain to fill the dry trap. If you see smoke indoors that is not due to a dry trap or that appears to be arising from the ground in your yard, call the Hillsborough Water Distribution and Collection Division at 919-296-9650 to have the problem investigated. The town will notify customers of private connection issues that require repair. The town will address issues with public sewer lines. For town and customers responsibilities, see the town Code of Ordinances, sections 14-21 and 14-22 . For more information, contact the utility maintenance supervisor at 919-296-9652. Wastewater Collection Division The Wastewater Collection Division cleans and repairs sewer lines and maintains sewage lift or pump stations. The town has: 100.82 miles of sewer lines, which includes: 84.06 miles of gravity sewer lines 16.76 miles of force main sewer lines 27 public pump stations 2,163 sewer manholes Awards In previous years, the Wastewater Collections Division and its staff have won awards from the N.C. American Water Works Association-Water Environment Association for: Outstanding Wastewater Collection Operator of the Year Small Wastewater Collection System of the Year

Fats, Oils and Grease Fats, oil and grease poured down the drain will collect and stick to plumbing and sewer lines. Over time, lines can become blocked, causing sewer backups or overflows. Properties that discharge greasy wastewater are required to have interceptors for fats, oil and grease. Residential customers can obtain a free fat trapper from the town. They also should: Discard used fats, oil and grease with other garbage or recycle at an Orange County solid waste convenience center. Avoid or limit use of garbage disposals. Scrape plates into trash cans. Use paper towels to wipe leftover oils and fats from pots and pans. Fat Trappers The town provides fat trappers to water and sewer customers to help keep grease and oils out of the sewer system. To receive a fat trapper or additional bags, contact the utilities infrastructure protection supervisor or visit the Town Hall Annex, 105 E. Corbin St., where water bills are paid. Video Fats, Oils and Grease Program No Wipes in the Pipes Only waste and toilet paper should be flushed. Household cleaning and personal hygiene products labeled as flushable or safe for sewer or septic systems do not dissolve. Additionally, do not dispose of trash, medicine or other items in the sewer system. These items clog sewer lines and can damage sewer pumps and other equipment. For more information, contact the utilities infrastructure protection supervisor. Video No Wipes in the Pipes

Shelters Emergency shelters in Orange County are provided by Orange County, Inter-Faith Council for Social Service and the Orange County Chapter of the American Red Cross. Cold Weather Shelters Cold Weather Cots is an emergency shelter program run jointly by Orange County and the Inter-Faith Council for Social Service. The program provides shelter for residents living unhoused during the winter. Inter-Faith Council for Social Service The IFC shelter locations are open every night November through March. Orange County The Orange County shelter location is open on nights when the temperature is at or below 32 degrees. People needing transportation to the county shelter may contact the county's street outreach team at 919-886-3351 by 6 p.m. each day for assistance. Men, women and families are welcome. Walk-ins are accepted. Cots, blankets and snacks are provided. Call 919-245-2490 to hear more information. Emergency Shelters Orange County officials work with the Orange County Chapter of the American Red Cross to open emergency shelters in two primary locations: Orange Middle School, 308 Orange High School Road, Hillsborough Smith Middle School, 9201 Seawell School Road, Chapel Hill Shelter Reminders Before and During Shelter Openings Shelters require residents to be as informed and prepared as possible. If you will need special assistance, call 919-245-2884 to register for assistance before a disaster strikes. For emergency transportation, call 919-245-6100. Shelter locations may change depending on the emergency. Listen to the radio for directions concerning shelter openings. Shelters will have food and water but will not have easy access to medications or other personal needs. Smoking is not allowed in shelters. See Prepare Your Pets for Disasters on Ready.gov. Orange County has the following regulations for animals at shelters: Service animals for the hearing and visually impaired are allowed in shelters. Orange County Animal Services staff will be on hand to board pets in the best manner possible. Owners of large animals and livestock should make preparations for their animals. Very limited support for these animals will be provided in a disaster.

Checklist of Steps to Open a Business Below are steps that must be taken when starting, expanding or relocating a business. See the checklist for detailed information. Determine Zoning District ― Get help from economic development staff in determining the zoning district most appropriate for your business type before you sign a lease, purchase a building or enter into a land agreement. Select Possible Sites ― Economic development staff can suggest possible sites for your business. The town works closely with the Orange County Economic Development Office to keep an updated inventory of available sites. Meet about Development and Occupancy ― Hillsborough economic development staff will assist you in setting up a meeting with town and Orange County staff to discuss property development, new construction or the upfit of space to be leased. The town contracts with the county for building inspection services. Items to be discussed include: Compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act, building codes and Health Department requirements for restaurants and food service establishments. Requirements for parking, lighting, landscaping, grading, grease traps, backflow prevention, fire access and fire suppression. Seek Permitting and Inspections ― Apply for all the permits necessary to start work on a space or to occupy the space once you've selected a site or existing building. These permits will have been discussed more extensively in the predevelopment meeting. Close the Project ― Economic development staff offer an optional meeting with business owners and developers at a project's conclusion to identify issues or challenges that may have impacted the project’s budget or timeline. The confidential meetings help improve the town's development processes. Step 1: Pre-development meetings — Town staff review the development process for the specific project and recommend how best to proceed. Step 2: Annexation or rezoning — The Hillsborough Planning Board reviews the proposed development and provides a recommendation to the Hillsborough Board of Commissioners, which then votes on the proposed development. Step 3: Public hearing — Some development activities are subject to public notice and public hearings. For items requiring public hearings, property owners within 500 feet of the subject property will receive a written notice. Additionally, signs are placed on the property indicating a public hearing is occurring and legal ads are posted in the local newspaper to inform residents.

The town often has major public projects that it is considering, planning or building. Projects are removed from this page after construction or the work is completed. The Public Space and Sustainability Division oversees most major town construction projects. See the Bid Postings page for bidding information on town projects. Town Projects Future Train Station — The town is working with the state to reestablish passenger rail service and provide for economic development in Hillsborough. It will use 20 acres that the town owns by the North Carolina Railroad corridor. See the Future Train Station project page. Lawndale Basin Sewer Rehabilitation — Sewer lines will be repaired and relined in the Lawndale Basin in northern Hillsborough. See the Lawndale Basin Sewer Rehabilitation project page. Parking Study — The town is comprehensively studying its parking supply and the demand for parking in the downtown area and West Hillsborough to address existing conditions and future needs. See the Parking Study page. Highway 86 North Facility — The facility will be renovated and storage outbuildings will be constructed to allow use by multiple town operations. See the Highway 86 North Facility project page. Ridgewalk Greenway — A feasibility study has been conducted on a future north-south greenway that would provide a bike/pedestrian route from the future train station to the downtown. See the Ridgewalk Greenway project page. River Pumping Station Relocation — The town is working to replace the 1970s-era River Pumping Station, moving it from the Eno River floodplain and increasing sewer capacity in the area. See the River Pumping Station Relocation project page. South Churton Street Multimodal Corridor Study — South Churton Street is being studied to develop design concepts that contribute to the town's character and meet the goals of a state-funded project to widen the road from Interstate 40 to the Eno River. Hillsborough offers many opportunities for recreation. It does not provide recreational programming. Town-maintained parks and greenways are open daily from 7 a.m. until 30 minutes after sunset. The Public Space and Sustainability Division: Manages town parks and greenways. Implements decisions of the Parks and Recreation Board . Gold Park includes swings and other play equipment. Parks and Recreation Board Proposed Greenway Reservations Riverwalk Greenway Town Map Town Parks and Greenways See the Town Map for directions and amenities. Greenways Parks Calvin Street Greenway — This short greenway allows pedestrian and bicycle access from downtown and adjacent neighborhoods to Gold Park and Riverwalk. Riverwalk Greenway — This greenway along the Eno River connects Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area and trails east of town. See the Riverwalk page. Community Parks Cates Creek Park — 1445 Cates Creek Parkway. This community park has a pollinator garden and a skate spot . The multi-use field with soccer goals can be reserved. See the Reservations and Bee City USA pages. Gold Park — 415 Dimmocks Mill Road. This community park includes a dog park and a part of the Riverwalk greenway. The multi-use field and large picnic shelter can be reserved. See the Reservations and Bee City USA pages. See the park's trail map . Natural Area Kings Highway Park — 1001 Ben Johnston Road. This natural area with trails is surrounded in part by Lake Ben Johnston. It includes a kayak launch . King St. Dog Park The dog park is a fenced-in area in Gold Park where dogs area allowed to be off leash. It has the same hours as Gold Park. Dog Park Rules Dogs must be: At least 6 months old and not in heat. Current on all required vaccinations, with rabies tags displayed. On a maximum 6-foot leash before entering and when leaving the facility. Within sight and under voice control of owner at all times. Immediately removed if showing aggression. Owners must: Collect and dispose of all dog waste. Help keep the off-leash area safe for all visitors. Report all dog bites to Orange County Animal Control. Call 919-942-7387 or 911. Ground Covering The dog park's ground is covered with shredded hardwood mulch that: Is safe for use by children and dogs. Helps reduce dust, dirt and the ground cover’s movement. Grass has not been planted because maintenance would be difficult with the park's heavy use and because establishing grass would require several seasons of nonuse. Self-Guided Walks Interpretive Signage The town's interpretive signage helps provide context to sites within Hillsborough. The signs provide understanding of the town's history, environment and culture. Most of the signs are along the Riverwalk greenway, but there are some at other key points of interest in town. See Signage Map Treasure Trees The Treasure Trees Program recognizes the preservation of significant trees in the Hillsborough area. Trees are selected by the Tree Board. View them on the Treasure Trees page. About Our Recreation No recreation is allowed at the town's reservoir. See the About Water page. Building in Flood-Prone Areas Undeveloped floodplains often serve the need for public parks and recreation. The Riverwalk greenway and Gold Park were built in their locations to provide recreation in areas that otherwise would not be developed. These recreation facilities require cleanup after a severe weather event to remove hazards. They are open for use many more days throughout the year than they are closed for weather and maintenance. Built to Withstand Flooding Riverwalk is located partially within Gold Park and was built along a sewer easement by the Eno River. Both recreation facilities were designed to withstand flooding. Gold Park’s dog park was built with a chain-link fence to allow floodwaters through. When flooding is expected, the fencing is left open to allow water carrying debris to flow through without damaging the fence. Severe Weather Parks and greenways are closed at times for the safety of the community and emergency workers. Hazards can exist even after a storm with high winds or snow has passed or after floodwaters have receded. Parks and greenways: Will remain closed following severe weather until the town can inspect the areas and remove any hazards. Are not a priority for snow and ice removal. They will be closed in deteriorating wintry conditions until staff determines they are safe. During Closures Heed any closure signs or barriers for parks and trails. Those who choose to use the town’s parks and greenways do so at their own risk. By entering closed areas and by moving or removing closure signs and barriers, you also: Slow cleanup efforts and delay the reopening of parks and greenways for everyone. Force public works and public safety staff away from other duties to reinstall closure signs and barriers. Force emergency workers away from other duties for potential rescues. Risk the safety of others. Subscribe to town news and follow @HillsboroughGov social media to stay informed about closures and reopenings. Shade at Parks Town staff and appointed boards are working to provide shade options at parks. Fast-growing shade trees have been planted around the perimeter of Cates Creek and Gold parks. Trees are planted in available spaces around the play areas but not inside due to spacing regulations for the play equipment. Because of the play equipment's current height and spacing regulations, sunshades in the play areas would be installed at a height that would provide little sun blockage during the day and that would make the shades a safety risk in high winds. Water Fountains Water is turned off at exterior drinking fountains at parks when the first freezing temperatures of winter are forecasted. Water service then is restored in the spring when the danger of freezing temperatures has passed. This helps avoid water line breaks, which can be costly to repair and disruptive to the use of recreational areas. Make a Recommendation The Tree Board makes planting decisions for town spaces. Plants typically are added between November and March to improve survival due to less heat and more precipitation. The Parks and Recreation Board advises the town on recreation improvements and implements recommendations in recreation master plans. Orange County provides recreational programming, a senior center and additional parks in and around town, including Fairview and River parks. Welcome to the Hillsborough Police Department in Hillsborough, North Carolina
I am honored to serve the Hillsborough community alongside a dedicated team of professionals who deeply care about the people we protect.
The department commits to excellence through our core values:
Community — Beyond just serving the community, the Police Department is an active member of the community and will contribute and engage.

Mission and Vision Mission The Hillsborough Police Department exists to make the Hillsborough vision a reality by providing exceptional service, protecting and enhancing our community, helping those in need, and exemplifying policing at its best through the most positive and professional law enforcement services possible. Vision The Hillsborough Police Department will be an example of the very best law enforcement service possible and will always strive to exceed our community’s expectations through our character, operations, interactions and personnel.

Internal Accountability The Police Department relies on an internal review process for accountability to policies, laws and best practices for the department's work. The internal review process addresses external complaints as well as incidents flagged internally for review. Every effort is made to investigate complaints from the community as completely as possible from the information provided. Example Internal Review Use of force is an example of an incident that may trigger an internal review. Department policy requires that use of force is reported for the display of a weapon toward a person and for any action that goes beyond the reasonably expected use of soft hands for guidance when detaining a person. Each incident of reported use of force is reviewed at several levels. A review generally includes: Viewing body worn camera footage. Reviewing statements of the officers, witnesses and suspects involved. Assessing any other possible evidence.

Ice and Snow Removal Pre-treatment If needed, the town will pretreat the following roadways with brine: A-E — Beckett’s Ridge Drive, Cameron Street, Cates Creek Parkway, College Park Road, East Corbin Street and Exchange Park Lane F-J — Hampton Pointe Boulevard and John Earl Street K-O — Lafayette Drive, Lakeshore Drive, East Margaret Lane, Meadowlands Drive and Millstone Drive R-Z — Rainey Avenue and Waterstone Drive Plowing Guidelines The town plows roadways to provide emergency responders with safe, timely access. Public Works employees monitor snowfall on pavement. Employees plow all town-maintained streets. They first plow town bridges, emergency services and the Orange County refueling station within the town limits. During heavy snow, employees work to keep priority areas clear. They plow the remaining town-maintained streets when weather conditions allow. Plowing is stopped if it does not clear roads or if it makes conditions worse. Responsibilities Roads and Driveways The state owns and maintains the main roads in town. The town does not clear driveways after plowing and does not maintain private streets. Parks, Greenways and Sidewalks Parks, greenways and sidewalks are not a priority for snow removal. The town will clear sidewalks around town facilities when time allows. The town does not remove snow or ice from residential sidewalks in town. Property and business owners are responsible for snow and ice removal from sidewalks in front of structures they own or occupy. Bulk Items The monthly collection occurs the second full week of the month. Sunday is considered the start of the week. See the curbside collections calendar for exact weeks. Bulk items may be placed by the street up to seven calendar days before the scheduled collection. The collection must fit into a pickup truck bed. A fee is assessed for items exceeding the typical load or for collection outside the regular collection week. See the special collections section. Bulk Items Collected Appliances Furniture Grills, if clean and free of charcoal and fuel tanks Mattresses Scrap metal, if clean Unmounted (rimless) tires Water heaters For questions about other items, contact the Public Works Division. Garbage Household garbage collection is provided once a week to single-family homes. Use town-provided carts. Each household is allowed up to two carts. For a second cart, see the sections on rollout carts and fees. Follow town requirements for when and how carts may be placed. See the section on rollout carts. Place only bagged household garbage in rollout carts. Dispose paint cans with household garbage if they are dried, flattened and lidless. Completely close the cart lid. Remove all rollout carts and uncollected trash from the street by 6 a.m. the day after collection. Garbage Items Not Collected The town does not collect the items below. Commercial Waste Independent vendors provide trash collection to multi-family housing communities, businesses, churches and nonprofits. Businesses may use any vendor they choose if town standards are met. See the regulations and an application for a dumpster exemption . Food Waste Composting food waste reduces disposal fees the town must pay and benefits the environment. Drop-off Sites Food waste can be dropped off for free at 11 sites in Orange County, including: Eno River Farmers Market in downtown Hillsborough. Orange County 24-hour recycling drop-off site in Hampton Pointe. Orange County waste and recycling center on Walnut Grove Church Road, north of Hillsborough. The North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality adds public and private composting sites to the NC Food Donation and Compost Resource Map as they become available. Acceptable Items Items that can be dropped off for composting at these sites includes: Food scraps. Food-related paper, including napkins, greasy pizza boxes and staple-free tea bags. Flowers and trimmings from small indoor plants. For more information on the drop-off sites and a comprehensive list of acceptable items, see the Orange County food waste page. Composting at Home Composting can be done at home and can reduce fertilizer, herbicide and water needs for plants. Learn how to get started on the Orange County Cooperative Extension website . For those without the space, conditions or desire for backyard composting, countertop composters can be purchased to provide a soil additive with less effort. Countertop composters may use a combination of grinders and heat to reduce food volume and create compost. Fees and Violations Fees can be paid several ways. Contact the administrative support specialist for more information. Cash or check at the Town Hall Annex, 105 E. Corbin St. Credit or debit card through the town's payments and donations website . Violations If requirements for collection are not followed, the garbage or bulk items will not be collected. An employee will leave information on the town's policy for the resident. If trash carts and uncollected garbage are not removed from the street as required, a notice of violation will be delivered to the resident by mail or by town staff. A fee of $25 per day will be assessed if the resident does not comply with the ordinance within five days of the notice date. Recycling and Other Solid Waste Services Orange County collects recycling at curbs on Wednesdays in Hillsborough. See the county's Urban and Town Curbside (Weekly Collection) page for requirements. The county also provides other trash services to Hillsborough residents. Contact Orange County Solid Waste Management for these services, including: Recycling drop-off sites. Household hazardous waste collection. Construction and demolition waste collection. Solid waste convenience centers. Rollout Carts For collection and safety, carts must be: Placed at the curb between 4 p.m. the day before collection and 6:30 a.m. the day of collection. Placed within 3 feet of the curb, with the handle facing away from the street. Placed at least 4 feet from parked cars, trees or other obstructions. Removed from the street by 6 a.m. the day after collection. See our video Position Your Solid Waste and Recycling Carts Properly . Rollout Cart Delivery and Repair Residents in single-family homes with active utility accounts may receive one free trash rollout cart after account activation if they live in town limits on a publicly owned road. See the Services for Your Property page to determine whether a property is in town limits. A fee is charged for a second cart. Payment must be received before delivery is scheduled. See the fees section for how to pay the fee. Place a work order or call the administrative support specialist to request: Cart delivery or repair Second cart

Flowers and trimmings from small indoor plants. For more information on the drop-off sites and a comprehensive list of acceptable items, see the Orange County food waste page. Composting at Home Composting can be done at home and can reduce fertilizer, herbicide and water needs for plants. Learn how to get started on the Orange County Cooperative Extension website . For those without the space, conditions or desire for backyard composting, countertop composters can be purchased to provide a soil additive with less effort. Countertop composters may use a combination of grinders and heat to reduce food volume and create compost.
Composting food waste reduces disposal fees the town must pay and benefits the environment.

Bagged Leaves and Grass The town collects leaves and grass clippings year-round in paper or biodegradable bags. Collection occurs on brush collection days. Up to 10 bags may be collected per household each week. Requirements Keep soil, trash and debris out of bags. Place bags: Within 4 feet of the curb but not on the curb. Where they do not interfere with traffic or water drainage. Where they do not block sidewalks, fire hydrants or water meters. Brush The town collects woody material from trees and shrubs weekly as part of its brush collection. Most homes receive collection on their regular garbage collection days. Homes on the following streets receive collection on Wednesday: Lydia and East Margaret lanes Streets including Caine, North and South Cameron, East Corbin, Huddle, East King, Mitchell, East Orange, East Queen, East Tryon, and East Union. Requirements Keep trash and loose leaves out of brush. Ensure brush is no larger than 6 feet in length and 6 inches in diameter. Place brush within 4 feet of the curb, 3 feet away from obstructions and not below trees or power lines. Stack limbs in one pile, with all limbs in the same direction. Place small amounts of brush in biodegradable paper bags. Or tie small amounts into bundles weighing less than 30 pounds. Use jute or sisal twine for the bundles. Do not use plastic or cotton twine. Allow a bagful or several armfuls of sticks to accumulate before placing at the curb. Christmas trees can be collected with brush with restrictions. See the Additional Information section. Loose Leaves The town collects loose leaves November through January. Collection occurs once per week, depending on the amount of leaves and weather. Collection does not occur on town-observed holidays. Requirements Keep trash, sticks and other debris out of loose leaves and bags. Place loose leaves and bags: Within 4 feet of the curb but not on the curb. Where they do not interfere with traffic or water drainage. Where they do not block sidewalks, fire hydrants or water meters.

Bill Adjustments for Leaks Customers may request an adjustment to their bills for leaks caused by water line breaks. One leak adjustment is allowed in a 12-month period. Account adjustments are not usually made for irrigation leaks. Billing and Adjustments Check for Leaks Fix leaks to save on utility bills. Nationally, 10% of homes have leaks of 90 gallons or more per day. Over a month, that's at least 2,700 gallons. A small drip from a worn washer can waste 20 or more gallons daily. Large leaks can waste hundreds of gallons daily. Check Around the House Check faucets and pipes. Replace worn washers immediately. Listen carefully for running water. Look for wet spots in your yard between the water meter and house. Regularly check your irrigation system for leaks. Check Your Bill A family of four's usage should be under 12,000 gallons in winter months. Look for significant changes from one month to the next.

In the Bathroom Reduce the amount of water used: Wet your toothbrush and then turn off the faucet. Rinse your razor in a partially filled sink instead of under a running tap. Shorten your shower. Cutting out one or two minutes can save up to 700 gallons of water each month. Take a shallow bath. This saves more water than a short shower. Install low-flow showerheads or flow restrictors. Install ultra-low flush toilets and faucets if building or remodeling a home. Reduce the amount of water flushed: Flush only when necessary and put trash in the trash can. Each flush wastes 5 to 7 gallons of water, and flushed trash can clog pipes. Put a filled plastic bottle in your toilet tank. Fill the bottle with water and a small amount of pebbles to weigh it down. Place it away from operating mechanisms. This can save you 10 or more gallons of water each day. Save water for other use: Place a bucket under the bath faucet when waiting for water to warm. Use the retained cold water later for house plants or to refill the toilet tank after flushing. Use water from pet dishes or dehumidifiers to water plants. In the Kitchen and Laundry Reduce the use of running water: Keep water in the refrigerator for drinking instead of running the faucet until water gets cold. Rinse vegetables in a pan of water. Defrost frozen foods in the microwave or refrigerator. Use the garbage disposal less. Consider composting. Putting food scraps and grease and oils down kitchen sinks risks clogging sewer pipes. Fill one sink with soapy water and one with rinse water when washing dishes by hand. If you have only one sink, use a dish rack and rinse with hot water. Use the smallest amount of detergent possible when washing dishes by hand. This reduces the amount of rinse water needed and the risk of clogged pipes. Use your dishwasher and washing machine for full loads only. If considering the replacement of large appliances: Select high-efficiency washing machines. Consider that new dishwasher models are more water- and energy-efficient. Outside and Dining Out If possible for outside plantings: Reduce or eliminate watering grass, bushes and plants. Reduce or eliminate planting new plants. If possible for outside maintenance: Avoid washing vehicles at home. Most commercial car washes recycle the wash water. Soapy runoff is not good for the environment or stormwater system. Consider delaying projects that use a lot of water, such as: Carpet cleaning with your own steam cleaner. Draining and refilling a hot water heater. Filling ponds, hot tubs, fountains or pools. Masonry projects that need a water mix for grout or concrete. Painting projects that require washing brushes, rollers and trays. Power washing. When dining out, if you: Won’t be drinking water, ask that no tap water be served. Will be drinking water, ask for bottled water during water restrictions.

Policy The mayor can issue a proclamation to restrict water use when water is in short supply in the Eno River, Lake Orange or the town's reservoir. The level of restrictions is determined by the available water supply. Construction-related activities that are not essential and that require water should not be undertaken during a declared water shortage. See the full drought policy . Stage 1: Voluntary Restrictions This stage begins when the town has less than 180 days of supply. Customers are encouraged in this stage to reduce water use by 10%. The town also may: Offer water-saving devices. Provide daily or weekly reservoir level and water usage statistics. Recommend water usage reduction techniques. Stage 2: Mandatory Restrictions This stage begins when the town has less than 135 days of supply. Customers must reduce water use by 10% and are encouraged to reduce use by 20%. No pressure washing or private car washing is allowed. Outdoor water use is limited to two days per week. Properties with odd-numbered street addresses may water on Tuesday and Saturday. Even-numbered properties may water on Wednesday and Sunday. The town must: Offer water-saving devices. Provide daily or weekly reservoir level and water usage statistics. Recommend water usage reduction techniques. Stage 3: Rationing This stage begins when the town has less than 90 days of supply. All customers must reduce water use by 30%, except for special medical use. Customers are not required to use less than the minimum usage billed. No outdoor water usage is allowed, other than for emergency use or fire protection. Irrigation water meters will be turned off or removed by the town. The town will: Lower water pressure in its distribution system by reducing tank storage levels to the extent possible. Capture any water flushed from water lines for water quality concerns and return it to the Eno River upstream of the town's raw water intake. Use other water sources if feasible, investigating such sources as rock quarries, ponds, springs, and other utility systems. Enhance public awareness of the daily water usage, reservoir level and goal for water usage.

Customers are not required to use less than the minimum usage billed. No outdoor water usage is allowed, other than for emergency use or fire protection. Irrigation water meters will be turned off or removed by the town. The town will: Lower water pressure in its distribution system by reducing tank storage levels to the extent possible. Capture any water flushed from water lines for water quality concerns and return it to the Eno River upstream of the town's raw water intake. Use other water sources if feasible, investigating such sources as rock quarries, ponds, springs, and other utility systems. Enhance public awareness of the daily water usage, reservoir level and goal for water usage.

Subscribe to news releases or sign up for emergency alerts . Keep Wipes and Other Trash Out of Pipes So-called flushable wipes do not break down in the sewer system. Post Date: May 13, 2026 8:00 a.m. Entangled wipes, plastics and other trash made this sewer pump at the Elizabeth Brady Pump Station inoperable in 2023, requiring replacement. Each pump costs about $34,000 and helps transport sewage to the Wastewater Treatment Plant. Did you know that wipes and other personal hygiene and cleaning products are the leading cause of clogged pipes? Only waste and toilet paper should be flushed. Items to Avoid Flushing Household cleaning and personal hygiene products labeled as flushable or safe for sewer or septic systems do not dissolve. They should always be placed in the trash. If your house is professionally cleaned, please ask the cleaning company to put these items in the trash: Floor cleaning pads, such as Swiffer wet or dry mopping cloths Disinfecting wipes Paper towels In addition to cleaning products, throw away the following: Tampons and pads Facial tissues Personal wipes Medicine These items and other trash clog sewer lines and can damage sewer pumps and other equipment. Costly Repairs Blocked pipes can lead to sewer overflows, which can be costly for you and the town’s utilities department. Consider the responsibilities: Your responsibility — Property owners are responsible for blockages in the sewer service line between the house or structure on their property and the public right of way or easement. The town can require installation or relocation of a cleanout at the right of way or easement if one is not present. Shared responsibility — The town owns and maintains the sewer main or sewer service line in public rights of ways or easements. It will clear blockages of lines in public rights of ways or easements. The town may require property owners to install or relocate cleanouts to the town's specifications. The town may agree to perform the work but may require reimbursement and the granting of property access from the customer. More Information See the town’s No Wipes in the Pipes video. For more information, contact the utilities infrastructure protection supervisor. Did you know that wipes and other personal hygiene and cleaning products are the leading cause of clogged pipes? The Utilities Department prepares water for drinking and cleans used water for return to the environment. It also maintains pipes and infrastructure to deliver drinking water and transport wastewater for treatment. See the Water and Sewer Services page for billing, rates, service connection and other services related to the water and sewer system. West Fork Eno Reservoir The Eno River is Hillsborough's source for water. No recreation is allowed at the reservoir. See how the town cleans the water for return to the Eno River. Sign Up Annual Reports Hillsborough's treatment plants regularly test for contaminants and prepare annual reports about their treatment processes and testing. Water Quality Report An annual report is published in July for the previous year. It includes  information on our water treatment system and performance as well as water quality information from the Environmental Protection Agency. Water Quality Report Wastewater Quality Report A report is published in August each year for the previous fiscal year (July 1-June 30). It includes information on our wastewater collection and treatment systems and their performance. Wastewater Quality Report Distribution and Collection Division The Water Distribution and Wastewater Collection Division: Repairs water line leaks. Cleans and repairs sewer lines. Maintains water tanks, booster pump stations and sewage lift stations. Staff members are responsible for programs and projects to maintain and protect the utility system. See: About Water About Wastewater Treatment Plants The town’s treatment plants prepare drinking water and clean used water. They regularly test for contaminants. Water Treatment Plant The water plant takes water from the Eno River, cleans and disinfects it, and then pumps it to customers. The state requires that the plant change its disinfection method for one month each year to clean the distribution system. About Water Wastewater Treatment Plant The wastewater plant removes waste and nutrients from used water, disinfects the water with chlorine, and then removes the chlorine before releasing the water into the Eno River. It does not include all actions taken at the meeting and should not be viewed as official minutes. The meeting is available to view on the town’s YouTube channel . See the agenda packet for more information. Proclamations The board approved proclamations for: Gun Violence Awareness Day — The day encourages support of local efforts to reduce gun violence and encourages residents to wear orange on June 5 to raise awareness about gun violence and to honor the lives of those lost to it. LGBTQ+ Pride Month — The month reflects on the rights movement for the community of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer and/or questioning, plus other sexual and gender minorities. It urges residents to recognize the contributions of the LGBTQ+ community and to promote principles of equality, liberty and justice in Hillsborough. Budget Work Session The board continued discussion on the town’s budget. See the news releases on the proposed budget and the budget public hearing . Property Tax The board continued discussion on the town’s tax rate, recommending a 2-cent increase to 53.3 cents to: Avoid using savings to fund the Fiscal Year 2027 budget and ensure adequate funds are available to respond to future needs and natural disasters. Reduce future tax rate increases related to major projects such as the train station, Ridgewalk greenway and downtown fire station. Prepare for possible state-imposed property tax restrictions. For property owners, the tax increase means $7.50 per month for those with a $450,000 home. Fees The board discussed fees and directed staff to increase several fees to help cover the costs associated with providing those services to the public. Fee increases include field and picnic shelter rental fees. Nonprofit Partnerships The board continued to discuss funding for local nonprofits and changed the following planned allocations in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget: Orange County Congregations in Mission — Increased to $21,000 Orange County Arts Alliance — Reduced to $0 The Arts Alliance was awarded $10,000 from the Hillsborough Tourism Development Authority at its May meeting. The town board directed the Hillsborough Arts Council to the Hillsborough tourism board and tourism development authority for fund requests in excess of $15,000. Data Centers The board held a public hearing before adopting a 60-day moratorium on data center development. The short-term pause allows the town time to complete the process required for a longer moratorium, during which the town intends to develop regulations for data centers. Software Management The board authorized the town manager to enter into an agreement with the North Carolina Department of Information Technology to use Tanium, a software that provides software update management and an overview of IT assets, including categorization and status of installed software. Police Conduct Home Security Checks Hillsborough police officers provide free home security checks and advice Post Date: May 27, 2026 8:30 a.m. Police Officer Jordan McDonald demonstrates a security check at a Hillsborough home. Whether you’re away for the day or for several weeks, the Hillsborough Police Department can help you make your home more secure. When requested, Hillsborough police officers will check on your home when you’re away and provide advice on how to make your property more secure before you go. “We want to do everything we can to help our residents,” said Police Sgt. Scott Foster, who leads the department’s community action team. “Our mission is to protect people and property.” According to a study by the home security company ADT, 65% of home break-ins occur during the day and more home burglaries occur in the summer than in other seasons. Asking the Police Department for help or following officers’ general tips may help save you the headache of a home break-in. Security and Property Checks When requested, an officer will visit your property as time permits and walk around the outside of your home. The time of the visit will be logged, and the visit will include visually checking that your windows and doors remain secure. For security assistance beyond two weeks, the Police Department offers a property check, which involves driving by your home as time permits but not necessarily walking on your property. In addition to giving you peace of mind, the frequent visits may deter someone from breaking in. They also provide a time frame for a break-in, should one occur. To schedule a security or property check, contact Senior Administrative Support Specialist Danielle King at least two business days before you plan to be away  at 919-296-9500 or by contact form . These services are secondary to primary emergency services but are still taken very seriously. A date, time or frequency cannot be guaranteed, but the Hillsborough Police Department does its best to maintain a high standard of customer service for these requests. Security Consultation Police officers also are available to meet with you to evaluate the security of your house and property and make suggestions. This consultation includes outside security considerations, such as fences, lighting and landscaping as well as doors, windows and locks. It also includes interior security, such as alarms, safes and how to best protect property inside the home. To request a security consultation, contact Foster by phone at 919-296-9563 or by contact form. General Security Tips Consider these simple tips to help secure your home. Outside: Lock up ladders — An unsecured ladder may be used to break into your home. Avoid hiding a key outside. Leave a key with a neighbor if you’re worried about locking yourself out. If you can, park your car in your garage while you’re away rather than in the driveway. Inside your home: Use a timer so lights come on at night, but don’t have only the hallway light on timer. Place a timer on a radio. Close blinds or drapes, or remove valuables from areas that can be seen through windows. In your garage: Lock garage doors. If your garage is attached to your house, lock the house door in your garage. Remove garage door opener remotes from any cars remaining on your property while you’re away. Other: Don’t post on social media that you’re on vacation. Test smoke alarms before going on vacation. Ask a neighbor to pick up your mail and packages. New Banners, Upcoming Banner Displays America 250, state, U.S. and pride banners will be displayed downtown this summer Post Date: May 21, 2026 10:15 a.m. The town has installed America 250 banners to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Hillsborough Public Works crews installed America 250 banners this morning. The new banners are part of the town’s celebration of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Crews will continue to change the banners affixed to utility poles on downtown streets through the rest of the year as Hillsborough observes multiple celebrations and honors Veterans Day in November. The schedule for changing banners is: May 21 to 29 — America 250 banners May 29 to June 12 — Pride flag banners to recognize Pride Month June 12 to 22 — U.S. and state flag banners to recognize Flag Day and Juneteenth June 22 to July 1 — Pride flag banners resumed for Pride Month July 1 to Nov. 9 — America 250 banners Nov. 9 — U.S. and state flag banners to recognize Veterans Day, followed by holiday wreaths The Hillsborough Board of Commissioners observes and honors many days throughout the year by issuing proclamations. Hillsborough to Observe Memorial Day on May 25 Town offices will be closed and solid waste collection adjusted Post Date: May 20, 2026 10:00 a.m. Town of Hillsborough offices will be closed Monday, May 25 to observe Memorial Day. Residential solid waste will not be collected that day. Residents whose garbage and yard waste are normally picked up on Mondays will receive service on Tuesday, May 26. Orange County will delay curbside recycling collection by one day next week. The county also will close its waste and recycling centers and its construction and demolition landfill on the holiday. Rollout carts may be placed by the street as early as 4 p.m. the day before collection. Please remove carts from the streetside by 6 a.m. the day after collection. Memorial Day Memorial Day is observed annually on the last Monday in May. It is a day of reflection and solemn observance to honor those in the armed forces who have lost their lives in service to their country. In a proclamation approved earlier this month by the Hillsborough Board of Commissioners, Mayor Mark Bell calls on community members to recognize and support the loved ones of the fallen and to reflect on their role in creating a more just, peaceful nation and world. A Memorial Day ceremony will be 8:45-10:15 a.m. May 25 at the Orange County Veterans Memorial, 2501 Homestead Drive in Chapel Hill. Hillsborough’s mayor will acknowledge the service branches at the start of the ceremony. He is a former member of the U.S. Naval Reserve. More Information For more information on: Residential garbage or yard waste collection, visit the town’s Garbage Collection page. Subscribe to news releases or sign up for emergency alerts . Town Board Meeting Summary Post Date: May 19, 2026 2:28 p.m. The draft budget includes funding a picnic shelter at Cates Creek Park. The Hillsborough Board of Commissioners met Monday, May 18 at the Town Hall Annex. Following is a brief summary. It should not be viewed as official minutes. The meeting is available to view on the town’s YouTube channel . See the agenda packet for more information. Budget Public Hearing Four community members spoke at the budget public hearing. Comments expressed included appreciation for: Major accomplishments in the past year. Keeping health insurance costs the same for town employees to cover spouses and dependents in the next fiscal year despite rising insurance costs. Budgeting design work for a sidewalk on Rainey Avenue for the next fiscal year with construction in Fiscal Year 2029. Providing financial support to the Hillsborough Arts Council. Budget Work Session The board asked questions about departmental requests in the proposed budget before sharing thoughts on major decision points. No votes were taken at this meeting. The board may choose to discuss the budget at its next work session at 7 p.m. Wednesday, May 27 and expects to adopt the budget June 8. The board meets in the Town Hall Annex, 105 E. Corbin St. See the news release on the manager’s recommended budget and financial plan for more detail including links to the recommended budget and a summary of the recommendation. Property Tax The draft budget was prepared without a proposed tax rate increase for Fiscal Year 2027, relying on deficit spending for all three years of the financial plan and reducing fund balance significantly by Fiscal Year 2029. The board discussed the proposal and recommended a two-cent rate increase for the upcoming fiscal year in order to eliminate the current year deficit, reduce future deficits and maintain healthy fund balance levels to ensure resiliency in the event of a natural disaster like the flooding caused by Tropical Depression Chantal in July 2025. Stormwater Fee The board supported the manager’s recommendation of a planned $15 increase in the residential stormwater fee with a proportional increase in the nonresidential stormwater fee. Water and Sewer Rates The board supported the manager’s recommendation of a planned 7.5% rate increase in water and sewer rates. Nonprofit Funding The board discussed and allocated funding for local nonprofits for the town’s Fiscal Year 2027 budget: Disability Awareness Council — $3,800 Exchange Club Park — $7,500 Fairview Community Watch —  $10,000 Food, Fitness and Opportunity Research Collaborative — $51,683 Hillsborough Arts Council — $15,000 Orange County Congregations in Mission — $11,000 Orange County Arts Alliance — $10,000 TABLE – $0 Storm Damage Reimbursement Assistant Town Manager Matt Efird shared the town’s progress in receiving reimbursement for damages and costs associated with the flooding caused by Tropical Storm Chantal. So far, the town has recovered about $2 million from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and insurance. The town expects to recover an additional $1.5 million in reimbursements and is continuing to seek additional funding for longer-term mitigation projects. Help the Hillsborough Tree Board eliminate Japanese knotweed, an invasive plant endangering native species.

The team gathers for two hours on Wednesdays, meeting in morning during the warmer months and in the afternoon in cooler months. Contact the Public Space and Sustainability Division to be connected.

The Historic District Commission reviews applications for exterior changes within the Hillsborough Historic District. A Certificate of Appropriateness or minor works approval from staff may be required before any exterior work can begin. All meetings are open to the public. The Historic District Commission approves changes to the district, including the addition of interpretive signs along the Riverwalk greenway. Agendas and Minutes Certificate of Appropriateness About the Historic District The Hillsborough Historic District was created in 1973 through passage of a preservation ordinance. The district presents a visual history of Hillsborough's development and includes the town’s commercial core and surrounding residential neighborhoods. The district is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and contains more than 100 houses, churches and buildings from the 18th and 19th centuries. Included is development from Georgian- and Federal-style buildings dating to the late 1700s to contemporary construction. The town's historic district overlaps with the National Register of Historic Places district, but it is a separate designation. Historic District Inventory Historic District Map About the Historic District Commission Mission The commission’s mission is to identify, protect and preserve Hillsborough's architectural resources and to educate the public about those resources and preservation in general. It conducts an awards program for noteworthy historic preservation projects in town. Role The commission has a quasi-judicial role. The commission: Hears evidence. Determines relevant facts. Ensures the changes are not conflicting with the special character of the historic district or landmark. Regulation It is against the law to begin building, moving, demolishing, altering or restoring any structure or site within the Historic District before a Certificate of Appropriateness has been issued by the commission or approved by staff as a minor work or ordinary maintenance and repair. See the Design Standards section on this page. Design Standards Exterior improvements to a site or structure in the Historic District may: Require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic District Commission. Be exempt from permitting. Be approvable as a minor works item by Planning and Economic Development Division staff. Before making any exterior changes to a site or structure, discuss the proposal with town staff to determine the process required for the project and to avoid potential after-the-fact permit penalties and enforcement. These standards and matrices guide the commission's decisions on Certificate of Appropriateness applications: Compatibility Matrix Historic District Design Standards (effective Sept. 3, 2021) Historic District Signage Matrix Membership Composition A majority of the commission’s members have specialized training or an interest in architecture, preservation, archaeology, history or building methods. Terms Members serve up to two consecutive three-year terms. One calendar year must pass before a member may be reappointed after serving two complete terms and any partial term. Read More The Planning and Economic Development Division issues zoning compliance permits for activities regulated under the Unified Development Ordinance that are requested on property in the town's limits and planning area. In some cases, a building permit may be required. The Orange County Planning and Inspections Department oversees building permits and inspections. Unified Development Ordinance Pay Online Pay by Other Methods Change of Use Permit Zoning compliance permits are issued for changes of use, such as moving a business into an existing non-residential retail or office space. Apply for Change of Use Permit Home Occupation Permit Before starting a home business, contact planning staff to describe the business you plan to open. Staff will help determine if the type of business you want to open meets conditions for a zoning compliance permit. The regulations guide and checklist below lists businesses prohibited from home occupation permits. Home Occupation FAQs Starting a Home Occupation Local Regulations Guide and Checklist Apply for Home Occupation Permit New Construction and Additions Permit Zoning compliance permits are issued for site changes, such as relocating or expanding an existing structure or constructing a new building, accessory building, deck or fence. See a sample plot plan . Apply for Permit Signs Permit Zoning compliance permits are issued before installing new signs or changing the location, sign face or message of an existing sign. Apply for Signs Permit Additional Information Accessory Dwelling Units Accessory dwelling units are secondary dwellings added to the property of a main dwelling. A dwelling unit must contain cooking, sleeping and bathing facilities. A kitchen must have cooking equipment and a sink. A bathroom must have a sink, toilet and shower or bathtub. Some neighborhoods have covenants that restrict multiple units. Property owners are responsible for checking with their homeowners association before applying for permits. Types of Accessory Units The town has defined two types of accessory units. Freestanding Units These include garage apartments or "granny flats." The parcel must be zoned Residential 10, 15 or 20 (R-10, R-15 or R-20). These designations are common to neighborhoods built before the town implemented special use zoning around the year 2000. Neighborhoods in special use zoning districts are not able to build freestanding units. They are built to higher densities and often don’t have lots large enough to accommodate a freestanding unit. These neighborhoods include Collins Ridge, Fiori Hill, Forest Ridge and Waterstone Estates. In-home Units These are fully attached to the main dwelling, such as an efficiency or basement apartment. The accessory unit must have its own exterior access. If interior access to the principal dwelling is provided, it must be lockable from both dwellings. Difference Between Zoning and Building Permits Building permits deal with compliance with the state building code for structural, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work. Orange County issues these permits and enforces these codes. The Town of Hillsborough issues zoning permits to verify that the use of a structure is allowed in a given district and that structures are not too tall or too close to the property line. Any project that changes the footprint of a structure or adds a new structure or fence requires a zoning permit if the lot is within the town’s planning jurisdiction. Interactive Zoning Map For detailed zoning information, use the town's interactive zoning map. See the guide for instructions. Use Interactive Zoning Map Submitting an Application Applications can be submitted: By email to planning@hillsboroughnc.gov. In person at Town Hall, 101 E. Orange St. By mail to Planning and Economic Development Division, PO Box 429, Hillsborough, NC 27278. Staff typically process permit applications in one to two business days.
