https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/about-us/: Private utility companies are installing gigabit fiber-optic cables throughout Hillsborough. The installations should bring more services, capabilities and choices for those living and doing business in our community. Fiber-optic cable installation near Churton Street Project Ownership The Town of Hillsborough is not performing or paying for this work. The installations are private projects owned and operated by the utility companies and their contractors. The state regulates excavation on public and private property to prevent damage to underground utilities. See more information on the North Carolina Law page of the North Carolina 811 website. Internet Service Providers Brightspeed Brightspeed has a Certificate of Public Convenience from the North Carolina Public Utilities Commission. This agreement allows the town 30 days to review plans, which must be approved if state conditions are met. Google Fiber The town has a master encroachment agreement with Google Fiber. Lumos The town has a master encroachment agreement with Lumos. Lumos is under contract with Orange County to provide broadband internet to rural areas. Spectrum Spectrum has expressed interest in bringing its fiber internet service to Hillsborough. The company has a franchise agreement with the state to provide video programming services. This agreement will allow the town 30 days to review plans, which must be approved if state conditions are met. Work within Public Rights of Way The utility companies have the legal right to operate within rights of way of the town and of the North Carolina Department of Transportation. The town can impose additional conditions in its rights of way through encroachment agreements with utilities that do not already have special agreements with the state. For utilities that have special agreements with the state, the town only may require utilities to keep roads functional, follow existing laws and repair any damage caused in the rights of way. Work on Private Property Any activity on privately owned property requires approval of the property owner. Utility companies may have legal right to operate in some private areas through a utility easement managed by a homeowners association or other private owner. The town does not have authority to regulate work on private property. This includes final connections between the street and house. What to Expect All Fiber Companies Subcontractors Subcontractors are performing the fiber installations for all internet service providers. The subcontractors should have proper identification with them at all times while performing work. Their vehicles should be marked with a legible magnetic decal or similar marking that identifies the vehicles as a subcontractor for the companies and provides a contact phone number. Markings Excavation requires notification to North Carolina 811 to allow utilities to mark underground lines for safety. The work may proceed if utilities have not been marked within the prescribed time period and if no visible indications of underground utilities exist at the site. Several weeks before construction, paint markings will be sprayed on the ground. The paint typically disappears in a few weeks. For more information regarding markings, see the North Carolina 811 website. Additionally, the town limits do not match Hillsborough's planning jurisdiction or water and sewer service areas. Find information about a property and the services offered there through the Orange County interactive zoning website . See the instructions below. Finding a Property Finding a Property To find a property on the zoning website: Enter the street address, owner name or parcel identification number in the appropriate search box. Click the Search button. The map will zoom to the location. Property information will appear in the Results tab on the left. If the website returns “0 records found,” your information may be out of date. Map Color Codes Dark Gray Background ― The property is in town limits. Light Gray Background ― The property is outside town limits but in the extraterritorial jurisdiction area. See the section on services outside town limits. Colored Background ― The property is outside town limits and the extraterritorial jurisdiction area. Zoom out of the map to better distinguish between the gray areas. Services Within Town Limits Services Within Town Limits If a property is within town limits, the town: Provides garbage collection . Provides law enforcement . Provides water and sewer service , if available. Fees and approval are required for any connections to the town's water and sewer system. Complete an availability inquiry to learn if water and sewer service is available. Oversees zoning. See the Zoning Compliance Permits page for more information and an interactive zoning map. Other agencies provide services in the town limits: Orange County provides recycling collection . Orange Rural Fire Department provides fire protection . Services Outside Town Limits Services Outside Town Limits The town has zoning jurisdiction within a limited area beyond town limits known as the extraterritorial jurisdiction area. For properties outside town limits, including those within Hillsborough's extraterritorial jurisdiction area, the town: May or may not provide water and sewer service . See the section on the water and sewer service area. Has a courtesy review agreement with Orange County for development projects and can provide recommendations. Charges fees for any connections to its water and sewer system. Fully reviews and determines approval of construction plans for any connections within a development project to its water and sewer system. This may include execution of a water and sewer extension contract. Other agencies provide safety and solid waste services: Private companies provide garbage collection. Orange County provides drop-off sites and recycling collection . Orange County Sheriff's Office provides law enforcement . Orange Rural Fire Department provides fire protection . Orange County oversees zoning for properties outside town limits and outside the town's extraterritorial jurisdiction area. Water and Sewer Service Area Water and Sewer Service Area The town's water and sewer service area extends beyond town limits. Once a property is found on the zoning website, do the following to determine whether it falls within the water and sewer service area: Click the Layers tab. Check the Water Sewer Jurisdictional Boundary box. Read the service designation for the property. Service Designations Hillsborough Primary Service Area ― Town water and sewer service may be available but not everywhere in this area. The town's comprehensive sustainability plan recommends reducing this area and following the plan's recommended development area. Hillsborough Long-Term Service Area ― Town water and sewer service does not extend into this area. Hillsborough is not focusing on expanding its system into this area. Service For questions about whether town water and sewer service is available for a specific property, complete the Water and Sewer Availability Inquiry . Properties outside the town water and sewer service area are overseen by one of the following: Orange County Environmental Health Division Orange-Alamance Water System Orange Water and Sewer Authority

https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/services/: Customers fund the operation of the town's water and sewer system, including the infrastructure needed to treat, transport and protect water. Please immediately call 911 to report any tampering or theft. See Fees and Charges Schedule for fees and penalties. See Utilities: Prohibited Activities in the Code of Ordinances. Water can be legally and safely obtained from a fire hydrant with an orange box. Billing and Adjustments Start or Stop Service Tampering and Theft of Infrastructure Backflow Prevention Devices The town own some backflow prevention devices on town properties. Most are privately owned. If you see anyone tampering with a backflow prevention device or have experienced a theft of the device: Call 911 to have an officer dispatched. Contact the utilities infrastructure protection supervisor. The devices are housed in utility boxes and prevent contaminated water from entering potable water in a building. They can be targets for theft due to their metal content. Property owners who have had a backflow preventer stolen or damaged will need to employ the services of a plumber. Preventing Theft Options for preventing theft include: Employing community or neighborhood watch prevention, asking community members to report any suspicious behavior to police. Adding a lock to the backflow preventer box or installing a locking box, available from a plumber or from a plumbing warehouse. If locks are added, access must be given to the town. Cutting back any shrubs or other plantings to allow some view of the device and ensuring that an area of at least 5 feet around the utility is free of any growth. Water Meters Any tampering of a meter or service connection will result in the meter being locked and a tampering fee and civil penalty. Service will not be reconnected until all fees are paid in full. Repeated tampering will result in removal of the meter, additional fees to reset and reactivate it, and potential civil or criminal charges. Theft of Water Safety and Operational Concerns Water theft can cause concerns for the public water system including: Water hammer (form of hydraulic shock) in the system that breaks pipes and damages equipment. Lowered water pressure for customers during the time of theft. Contamination of the public water system. Costs associated with repairing damage to the system. Theft from Hydrants If you see a person or business taking water from a water hydrant without an orange meter box, report it immediately to 911 and to the utility system superintendent. To help the town prosecute the case: Discreetly take a photo if possible. Note the time, date, location, vehicle name and number, and license plate. Legally Obtained Water Contractors are able to purchase bulk water from the town. They can: Obtain water from the Water Treatment Plant by paying in advance at the Town Hall Annex. Rent water meters to legally obtain water from a fire hydrant. The meters are housed in an orange box with a backflow prevention device to safely obtain water. See the Start or Stop Service page. Contact Information Adron F. Thompson Facility, 715 Dimmocks Mill Road 919-296-9650 Office Hours — 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday-Friday. Emergencies Tampering or Theft — Call 911 and then use the contact utilities form. Water and Sewer Emergencies — Report immediately by calling 919-732-3621. https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/about-us/: Staff from the Budget Division and Financial Services Department manage the budget and finances for the town. Two volunteer boards also have annual budgets to handle funds they oversee: the Tourism Board and Tourism Development Authority . Nonprofit Partnerships Stormwater Fees Tax Rates and Compliance Water and Sewer Rates Budget Budget Budget The budget is a financial plan for the fiscal year (July 1-June 30). Hillsborough uses a three‐year format to better see any fiscal or operational challenges.  The budget's first year is legally binding. Years 2 and 3 show needs to plan for. The budget contains: An estimate of proposed expenditures. The proposed means of financing the expenditures. Goals and objectives of the expenditures. The Budget Division is responsible for preparing the town's budget. When possible, the town applies for federal, state and other grants to cover some of the cost of town projects. Manager's Recommended Budget Fiscal Year 2027 Budget and Financial Plan Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Message Fiscal Year 2027 Budget at a Glance Current Budget Fiscal Year 2026 Budget Ordinance Fiscal Year 2026 Budget and Financial Plan Fiscal Year 2026 Budget at a Glance Fiscal Year 2026 Fees and Charges Schedule Fiscal Year 2026 Budget Message Budget Process The budget process takes nearly eight months. November — Town staff begin working on budget proposals for the next fiscal year, which starts July 1. January-March — The mayor and commissioners meet with key staff members in a retreat during the winter to plan for the budget. The retreat gives staff guidance on the priorities and direction for the budget. May — The town manager presents a recommended budget to the town board. The community is invited to review and share comments on the budget at a public hearing later in the month. The board also conducts a work session to discuss the budget at the same meeting. June — A second work session occurs in June if needed. The board votes on the budget at a regularly scheduled meeting in June. July — The approved budget goes into effect on July 1. Funds The town’s three budgetary funds are the General Fund, Stormwater Fund, and Water and Sewer Fund. General Fund — Primarily funded with property and sales tax revenues and pays for services like police protection, residential garbage collection and building and maintenance of recreation facilities. Stormwater and water and sewer funds — Enterprise funds that rely on user fees to pay for their specific services. No profits are made in enterprise funds, and the revenue is used for no other purpose. Strategic Plan The town uses a strategic plan to align available resources with priorities. The plan is used in coordination with the budget and the Comprehensive Sustainability Plan. Strategic Plan Comprehensive Sustainability Plan Financial Report Annual Financial Report The Annual Comprehensive Financial Report is a complete set of the town's financial statements for the previous fiscal year (July 1-June 30). The Financial Services Department oversees preparation of the annual report. Tourism Board activities are supported from a 1% tax on prepared food and beverages. Tourism Development Authority activities are supported from a 3% room occupancy tax. Hillsborough Water Orange County Learn More Boil Water Advisory Boil Water Notice About OC Alerts OC Alerts is a mass notification system that is a partnership of Orange County, the towns in the county and Orange Water and Sewer Authority, which provides service to the Carrboro and Chapel Hill area. OC Alerts is on the Everbridge platform. It is separate from the Town of Hillsborough's utility billing system. Alerts can be received via phone calls, text messaging and email based on locations you care about. January 02, 2026 8:00 a.m. More News Lead is not typically found in raw water sources, such as lakes, but it can enter drinking water from corrosion of plumbing materials that contain lead. The town adds the corrosion prohibitor orthophosphate into drinking water to prevent corrosion in plumbing materials. Identify Your Service Line Material Water Service Line Material Form Water Service Line Map About Lead in Water Across the country, service lines commonly were made from lead pipe from the late 1800s, throughout much of the 20th century, and in some cities as late as the mid-1980s. After June 1986, installation of new lead service lines was prohibited. Regulations Safe Drinking Water Act In 1974, the U.S. Congress passed the Safe Drinking Water Act, which requires the Environmental Protection Agency to determine the safe levels of contaminants in drinking water. The safe level of lead in drinking water is zero. Congress later amended the act — effective after June 1986 — to prohibit using pipes, solder or flux that contain lead in public water systems or in plumbing in facilities that provide water for human consumption. Federal Lead and Copper Rule In 1991, the Environmental Protection Agency published the lead and copper rule to minimize these heavy metals in drinking water. The rule established a maximum contaminant level goal of zero for lead in drinking water and a treatment technique to reduce corrosion of lead and copper pipe materials within water distribution systems. Rule Revisions In 2021, the Environmental Protection Agency revised the Lead and Copper Rule to improve protection of public health. The revisions focus on: Identifying and removing lead service lines. Providing increased levels of protection from lead exposure in drinking water to children at schools and childcare facilities. Providing information about lead in drinking water to the community. The revised rules required water systems to develop a publicly available inventory of public and private water service lines and their makeup by Oct. 16, 2024. The inventory must be updated annually. Any unknown materials must be identified within 10 years of the initial inventory compliance date. Resources For more information, see these resources from the Environmental Protection Agency: Safe Drinking Water Act page Lead and Copper Rule page Infographic — Improving Lead Sampling to Better Protect Public Health News Release — EPA Finalizes Historic Action to Better Protect Children's Health Harmful Effects Harmful Effects Lead in drinking water has the following negative effects, according to the Environmental Protection Agency: Children Even low levels of lead in the blood of children can result in: Behavior and learning problems Lower IQ and hyperactivity Slowed growth Hearing problems Anemia In rare cases, ingestion of lead can cause seizures, coma and death. Pregnant Women Lead can accumulate in our bodies over time, where it is stored in bones along with calcium. During pregnancy, lead is released from bones as maternal calcium and is used to help form the bones of the fetus. This is particularly true if a woman does not have enough dietary calcium. Lead also can cross the placental barrier exposing the fetus to lead. This can result in serious effects to the mother and her developing fetus, including: Reduced growth of the fetus Premature birth All Adults Adults exposed to lead can suffer from: Cardiovascular effects, increased blood pressure, and hypertension Decreased kidney function Reproductive problems (in both men and women) Resources For more information, see these resources from the Environmental Protection Agency: Learn About Lead webpage Inventory in Hillsborough Lead in Hillsborough Town records dating to the mid-1930s call for copper or plastic water service lines and not lead. Lead service lines have not come up in staff discussions with local plumbers familiar with the area and have not been found by staff when working throughout the system. Homes and buildings built before 1987 may have lead service lines. Inventory The Hillsborough Utilities Department has developed an inventory of water service line materials in the community to help identify any lead service lines. The Environmental Protection Agency required the initial inventory by Oct. 16, 2024, under revised requirements to the Lead and Copper Rule. Updates must be made each year, and unknown materials must be identified within 10 years. Community Help For some properties, town staff continue to need community members’ help in identifying or correcting the materials of their private water service lines. Private lines are those between the building and water meter. In this inventory, the service line is under 2 inches in diameter. Please check the town’s Water Service Line Map to see if your building’s service line is marked as unknown. If the town does not have information about the customer side of your water service line, please determine the material by checking inspection reports for your home or building or by performing simple tests on the Identify Your Service Line Material page. Once you have identified your pipe material, complete the Water Service Line Material Form . Attach documentation of your service line material, such as a photo, and any repairs made to the service line after 1986 for homes or buildings built before 1987. Water Service Line Map Instructions Use the Water Service Line Map to see if the service line material at your property has been identified. Enter your address in the search field at the top of the map. Your property will become highlighted on the map. A circle at the property will display materials for both sides of the service line — utility and customer sides. See the map’s legend for the color coding of your circle. The circle’s left side represents the water service line owned by the town. The circle’s right side represents the water service line owned by the customer. If the material is unknown or incorrect, the town needs your help in identifying the material or reporting the correct material. A circle with gray on the right side means the town does not have information on the water service line for that property. Precautions Precautions the Town Takes Corrosion Inhibitor The town adds a blended phosphate corrosion inhibitor to its water. This additive greatly reduces the risk of pipes leaching lead and copper into water on the public and private side of water lines. A building’s supply lines and plumbing are not owned by the town. Periodic Testing The town performs periodic testing of customers’ water, primarily conducting tests in houses built during the years that lead-based solder was in use. Use of lead-based solder was a major reason the Environmental Protection Agency instituted the Lead and Copper Rule in 1991. The Lead and Copper Rule requires that the town check the amount of lead and copper in water after the water has passed through a customer’s service line and building plumbing. The town tests 30 samples every three years. The Environmental Protection Agency has reduced the testing required of the town due to its long history of compliance with the Lead and Copper Rule, which the agency has revised several times. The town has remained fully compliant since the rule was created. Pipe Materials Replacement Lead particles can attach to galvanized pipes, which were commonly used for water mains several decades ago. The town has a program to replace galvanized water mains on the public side of the water meter with newer standard materials when galvanized pipes are found. Precautions Customers Can Take If your home or building was built before 1987, you may have a lead service line. To determine your service line material, check inspection reports for your structure or v isit the Identify Your Service Line Material page for guidance on testing your line. See other precautions below. Internal Water Testing Homes and buildings may have internal plumbing materials that contain lead. Testing can determine whether lead is in your drinking water. The town offers free water testing to determine if lead is in your drinking water. For testing, utilities staff must be given access to the interior of your building. Before requesting a water test, please check the Water Service Line Map to see if the material of your property’s water service line has been identified. Testing performed by commercial laboratories generally costs between $20 and $100. For more information, see these resources from the state and Environmental Protection Agency: Certified Drinking Water Commercial Laboratories Home Water Testing Protect Your Tap: A Quick Check for Lead Tips to Limit Exposure Customers who suspect they have lead pipes or copper pipes with lead-based solder are encouraged to take the following additional precautions to limit exposure: Flush water lines after a period of stagnation. For guidance, see the Stale Water section on the About Water page. To minimize waste, consider using the released water to flush toilets or water plants. Purchase a filtering water pitcher certified to remove lead. Purchase a whole house filtering or treatment device certified to remove lead. Make sure it is properly installed and maintained. Note that a filter prevents the town from conducting bacteriological tests of a property’s water lines should a water quality issue occur. This is because the water will have undergone secondary treatment, and test results would not provide data on the water Hillsborough delivers. Regularly clean the screen or aerator on faucets. Sediment, debris and lead particles can collect. Contact Information Town Hall Annex, 105 E. Corbin St. 919-296-9630 Office Hours — 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday-Friday Please make an appointment for in-person visits. Corrosion Inhibitor The town adds a blended phosphate corrosion inhibitor to its water. This additive greatly reduces the risk of pipes leaching lead and copper into water on the public and private side of water lines. A building’s supply lines and plumbing are not owned by the town. Periodic Testing The town performs periodic testing of customers’ water, primarily conducting tests in houses built during the years that lead-based solder was in use. Use of lead-based solder was a major reason the Environmental Protection Agency instituted the Lead and Copper Rule in 1991. The Lead and Copper Rule requires that the town check the amount of lead and copper in water after the water has passed through a customer’s service line and building plumbing. The town tests 30 samples every three years. The Environmental Protection Agency has reduced the testing required of the town due to its long history of compliance with the Lead and Copper Rule, which the agency has revised several times. The town has remained fully compliant since the rule was created. Pipe Materials Replacement Lead particles can attach to galvanized pipes, which were commonly used for water mains several decades ago. The town has a program to replace galvanized water mains on the public side of the water meter with newer standard materials when galvanized pipes are found.

Internal Water Testing Homes and buildings may have internal plumbing materials that contain lead. Testing can determine whether lead is in your drinking water. The town offers free water testing to determine if lead is in your drinking water. For testing, utilities staff must be given access to the interior of your building. Before requesting a water test, please check the Water Service Line Map to see if the material of your property’s water service line has been identified. Testing performed by commercial laboratories generally costs between $20 and $100. For more information, see these resources from the state and Environmental Protection Agency: Certified Drinking Water Commercial Laboratories Home Water Testing Protect Your Tap: A Quick Check for Lead Tips to Limit Exposure Customers who suspect they have lead pipes or copper pipes with lead-based solder are encouraged to take the following additional precautions to limit exposure: Flush water lines after a period of stagnation. For guidance, see the Stale Water section on the About Water page. To minimize waste, consider using the released water to flush toilets or water plants. Purchase a filtering water pitcher certified to remove lead. Purchase a whole house filtering or treatment device certified to remove lead. Make sure it is properly installed and maintained. Note that a filter prevents the town from conducting bacteriological tests of a property’s water lines should a water quality issue occur. This is because the water will have undergone secondary treatment, and test results would not provide data on the water Hillsborough delivers. Regularly clean the screen or aerator on faucets. Sediment, debris and lead particles can collect.

https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/community: The town is working to add a booster pump to improve the interconnection between the town's water supply and the Orange Water and Sewer Authority's supply in southern Orange County. Location and Background The booster pumping station is to be built off Old N.C. 86 near Starfield Circle, south of Hillsborough. The station will improve a connection that already exists between the town's water supply and Orange Water and Sewer Authority's supply on the south side of Hillsborough. The improved connection is expected to meet the water demands of either utility during a drought or an emergency. The station would benefit the entire town and specifically help serve the UNC Hospitals Hillsborough Campus and Orange County/Hillsborough Economic Development District on the town's south side in an emergency due to the planned location near receiving pipes. Funding The estimated cost of the project is $2.2 million. Grant Funding The town received a Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities grant of $1.01 million from the Federal Emergency Management Agency in August 2023. As a part of the grant, the town would pay for 30% of the project. In April 2025, the federal program was ended and all applications from fiscal years 2020-2023 were canceled. This canceled $831,418 in federal funds for the building of the booster pumping station. North Carolina and 19 other states sued FEMA in July 2025 over its decision to cancel the BRIC program. In December 2025, a U.S. district court judge ruled the program was unlawfully ended. On March 18, 2026, FEMA issued an advisory notifying states that the agency plans to resume programming support. As of June 2026, the BRIC program has been reestablished, and the town has received reimbursements from FEMA for expended design fees. The state plans to transfer the project to its hazard mitigation grant program. Moving the project to the state's program would give the town more time to complete the project and include increased costs. Current Phase The project is  in the design phase. Additionally, permitting and easement acquisition are not complete. Staff Title Phone Email Strandwitz, Marie Utilities Director 919-296-9631 Email

https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/about-us/: Hillsborough's drinking water comes from the Eno River. Before the water is safe to drink, it must go through multiple stages of treatment, which can take several days. The Water Treatment Plant is staffed 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Staff who maintain the pipes, pumps and tanks connected with supplying water to you must be available at all hours for emergencies. About Water Alerts Backflow Prevention Lead and Drinking Water Water Conservation Our Drinking Water Source Eno River, Lakes and Reservoir The Eno River is Hillsborough's water source. Water from the river is drawn from three sites located in the Upper Neuse River watershed. The Eno and these three sites are considered surface water — natural water that has not penetrated much below the ground. Lakes on the Eno River Lake Ben Johnston — Hillsborough takes water from this lake to make drinking water. Seven Mile Creek enters the Eno River upstream of this area. Lake Orange — The town uses this lake as a secondary source of water from the Eno. The lake is on the east fork of the river outside town limits. It is maintained by Orange County. West Fork Eno Reservoir The town owns this reservoir on the west fork of the Eno River in nearby Cedar Grove and uses it as a secondary source for water. It can store about 1.2 billion gallons of water. The reservoir opened in 2000, and a second phase was completed in 2021. It includes an innovative spillway that provides more surface in a compact area for water to spill over. The dam resembles piano keys when in use. Emergency Water The town has pipe connections with neighboring utilities to receive or send water during emergencies. Receiving Water Hillsborough can receive water from Durham in an emergency. Additionally, the Hillsborough Utilities Department is working on a project that would enable the town to receive water from its southern utilities neighbor, Orange Water and Sewer Authority. Sending Water Hillsborough can send water to: City of Durham Water Management Orange-Alamance Water System, which serves some rural areas in Orange and Alamance counties Orange Water and Sewer Authority, which serves the Carrboro and Chapel Hill area History of the Reservoir In the 1980s and early 1990s, the Hillsborough community began exploring options for addressing the town’s water shortage due to a history of droughts and water restrictions and a desire to accommodate expected future growth. In 1993, Hillsborough voters approved general obligation bonds to help pay for building the reservoir’s first phase. The first phase was built with expansion in mind. The reservoir’s 20-year permit allowed for a second phase to be started by 2018. In 2000, the reservoir was made operational earlier than scheduled and before full to help provide immediate drought relief for customers under water restrictions. Severe Droughts Hillsborough experienced severe droughts in the 1920s, 1930s, 1950s, 1980s and 2000s. In 1954, schools closed at noon and the town sought federal aid because of drought conditions. That same year, drought conditions forced the town to disconnect the water of any customer found wasting it. In 1988, mandatory water restrictions were put in place. By the early 1990s, the town completed an interconnected pipeline with the City of Durham to allow regular purchases from Durham’s water system to withstand periods of droughts and water restrictions. The town could only purchase water between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. due to demands on Durham’s system. Benefits Phase 1 of the reservoir has: Helped the town withstand several severe droughts in the 2000s. At one point, larger surrounding systems were near or below 50 days of remaining water, but Hillsborough still had enough water for 200 days. Allowed Hillsborough to accommodate new development. Many residents and businesses joining Hillsborough after 2000 would not be here today without the reservoir. The Phase 2 expansion of the reservoir: Is a long-term investment in Hillsborough’s water supply. Raised the reservoir about 10 feet, doubling its volume and providing a maximum yield of 6 million gallons of water per day. No Recreation on the Reservoir Recreation is not allowed at the West Fork Eno Reservoir or the surrounding town-owned property. This includes boating, hunting and fishing. Required Conservation Federal and state permits require a conservation easement to: Protect the town’s drinking water source. Reduce the effects of the reservoir on others. To provide a 100-foot buffer around the reservoir, the town must keep the land in a natural state with no development, recreation or access other than to maintain the reservoir. Risks The town does not have the resources to oversee public activities at the reservoir and cannot assume the risk or liability of allowing recreational activities. Recreation also could introduce invasive animals and plants. The town already funds treatment to remove a weed native to South Asia that can damage utility equipment and the environment. See the section on annual treatment for an invasive plant on this page. Seasonal Treatment for Hydrilla The state does not plan to treat the Eno River for hydrilla in 2026 due to the flooding from Tropical Storm Chantal in 2025. A survey will be conducted later this year to determine whether hydrilla treatment should resume. Typically, the state annually treats 16 miles of the Eno River with the herbicide fluridone to reduce hydrilla, an invasive aquatic plant. Applications typically start in mid-May and continue through August. The section of the river treated is below the Ben Johnston Lake dam in Orange County to Roxboro Road and U.S. 501 in Durham County. The herbicide is applied in a concentration that is safe for humans, fish and wildlife and well below limits set by the Environmental Protection Agency. Property owners next to the treated section of river should use caution in using river water for irrigation during this time. About Hydrilla Hydrilla is native to South Asia and grows rapidly, creating thick mats on the surfaces of lakes, rivers and other waterways. The weed: Negatively affects the health of fish and wildlife in the area. Can clog intakes for supplying drinking water and irrigation. Can harbor mosquitoes. Can interfere with recreation on waterways. The plant was discovered in the Eno River watershed in the early 1990s in Lake Orange, which is upstream of Hillsborough and one of the town's water sources. In 2009, biologists confirmed hydrilla in the West Fork Eno Reservoir. The town-owned reservoir is stocked with triploid grass carp to manage the invasive plant. More Information The North Carolina Division of Water Resources manages the annual treatment. Hillsborough helps fund it. For more information, contact Stormwater and Environmental Services Manager Terry Hackett by email or phone at 919-296-9621. Water Treatment Our Water Quality The town's water treatment must meet high standards set by the town, state and federal governments. Hillsborough routinely tests for more than 150 substances in the town's drinking water and meets or exceeds the standards. See the annual Water Quality Report . Water Plant Testing Staff monitor and evaluate water 24 hours a day. The plant has: A state-certified laboratory to test for bacteria daily. Two lab-certified operators who test raw and finished water at the plant every two hours — more than required by the state. Water System Testing Staff also test various points in the water system. The water system includes the pipes, pumps and tanks needed to transport and store water. Tests occur: Weekly — For bacteria at five of the farthest points in the town's water lines. Monthly — For bacteria at 15 areas. Quarterly — For disinfection byproducts. These are substances created by the process to clean water. Annually — For inorganic materials, pesticides, synthetic organic chemicals, nitrates, volatile organic compounds and secondary contaminants. Every five years — For unregulated contaminants that the Environmental Protection Agency lists for testing. Our Water Treatment Process The Hillsborough Water Treatment Plant is the processing plant for your water. The plant takes raw water from the Eno River. It then adds ingredients and applies processes to the water to make it usable. The plant focuses on: First — Cleanliness and compliance with standards. Second — Taste, odor and appearance. Water Treatment Converting raw water into drinking water includes injecting chemicals at multiple points to help remove organic material, disinfect the water and ensure longer freshness before releasing it for use by the community. The chemical process starts before the raw water reaches the Water Treatment Plant. Water released from the town's reservoir travels to Lake Ben Johnston, where the town removes water for use. At this intake location, a chemical is added to help particles in the water combine for easier removal. At the plant, more chemicals are added for the same reason and to adjust the water's color, acidity and alkalinity. Filtering Out Materials The water then goes through several filtration, aeration and clarification stages. In these stages, the water remains in large basins while being mixed at slower and slower speeds. This allows the combined large materials to drop to the bottom of the basins. Finally, the clear water moves through a fine filtration system to remove remaining particles. At this stage, the water’s turbidity is measured and filtration adjustments are made to remove any cloudiness from the water caused by large amounts of particles that are otherwise invisible to the eye. Adjusting Treatment The water is then disinfected and final adjustments to acidity and alkalinity are made before the water is pumped through pipes to homes and businesses. Throughout the treatment process, employees test the water for more than 150 contaminants, making adjustments to the treatment as needed. See: From River to Faucet: Hillsborough's Water Treatment Process video Water Treatment Plant and Tours The Water Treatment Plant employees are highly certified. They continually operate and maintain the plant 24 hours a day to ensure compliance with state and federal permits and regulations. The plant can treat up to 3 million gallons of drinking water per day. Awards In previous years, the Water Treatment Plant and its staff won an award for Outstanding Operator of the Year from the N.C. Waterworks Operators Association. Tours See what it takes to prepare water taken from the Eno River for drinking. Public tours are offered at 1 p.m. on the second Friday of the month in March and September. Private tours can be scheduled separately for special groups. All tours are open to a maximum of 10 people with participants at least 10 years old. All tours require complete a request form. Request a Tour Water Distribution  and System Maintenance Annual Chlorine Disinfection For one month each year, the town is required to disinfect drinking water with chlorine. The state requires this annual change in utilities that normally use chloramines, a compound of chlorine and ammonia. Chlorine is a more intense disinfectant, and the annual change helps ensure a high level of disinfection in water mains. Other utilities in the region conduct the disinfection at the same time. This includes Hillsborough’s interconnected neighboring utilities, Orange Water and Sewer Authority and the City of Durham. Effects on Customers During the annual disinfection, some customers may notice a chlorine taste or odor in Hillsborough’s drinking water. Your water remains safe to drink. To remove chlorine taste and odor from water, you can: Add a few lemon slices to a pitcher of water. The lemon’s ascorbic acid will neutralize the chlorine. Let water sit in an open container in the refrigerator or on a counter for a day or so. A wide or shallow container will allow more contact between the air and water. Filter water with activated carbon. Water pitchers with such filters are sold locally. Boil water for 15 minutes to evaporate the chlorine. If you use Hillsborough water for special purposes or for processes involving careful control of water characteristics, the town encourages you to seek advice from an appropriate technical source — such as a filter vendor or service company — about whether and how to make adjustments to your use of Hillsborough water during the month of chlorine disinfection. Annual and Periodic Water System Flushing During the annual disinfection, staff release water from fire hydrants to ensure chlorine flows through the entire system. They also perform maintenance on hydrants. The annual flushing helps remove sediment and other minerals that may have settled in the water system. This flushing can cause temporary cloudiness or discoloration of water and could discolor light-colored fabric. If discoloration or air bubbles appear in the water, customers should run cold water in a bathtub for a few minutes until the water and air bubbles clear. If the water does not clear within five minutes, contact the Water Treatment Plant at 919-732-3621. During flushing or hydrant maintenance: Town personnel may be required to trim plantings or remove other items to ensure that adequate access to the hydrants exists for emergencies and maintenance. Community members may be asked to relocate plants and other items in street rights-of-way where necessary to provide a clear, 3-foot-wide area around a hydrant. More Information Black Residue Black residue around utility fixtures generally does not indicate a problem with water quality. It is likely due to one of the following: Bacteria feeding on oxidized iron and manganese in water. Stale Water Before resuming use of a building or during periods of underutilized use, remove stale and potentially unhealthy water in your building’s water system by flushing the water system and all water devices. Background When buildings are vacant or operating at significantly reduced capacity for more than a few days, water sits in pipes and devices instead of flowing. Hillsborough's drinking water comes from the Eno River. Before the water is safe to drink, it must go through multiple stages of treatment, which can take several days. The Water Treatment Plant is staffed 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Staff who maintain the pipes, pumps and tanks connected with supplying water to you must be available at all hours for emergencies. About Water Alerts Backflow Prevention Lead and Drinking Water Water Conservation Our Drinking Water Source Eno River, Lakes and Reservoir The Eno River is Hillsborough's water source. Water from the river is drawn from three sites located in the Upper Neuse River watershed. The Eno and these three sites are considered surface water — natural water that has not penetrated much below the ground. Lakes on the Eno River Lake Ben Johnston — Hillsborough takes water from this lake to make drinking water. Seven Mile Creek enters the Eno River upstream of this area. Lake Orange — The town uses this lake as a secondary source of water from the Eno. The lake is on the east fork of the river outside town limits. It is maintained by Orange County. West Fork Eno Reservoir The town owns this reservoir on the west fork of the Eno River in nearby Cedar Grove and uses it as a secondary source for water. It can store about 1.2 billion gallons of water. The reservoir opened in 2000, and a second phase was completed in 2021. It includes an innovative spillway that provides more surface in a compact area for water to spill over. The dam resembles piano keys when in use. Emergency Water The town has pipe connections with neighboring utilities to receive or send water during emergencies. Receiving Water Hillsborough can receive water from Durham in an emergency. Additionally, the Hillsborough Utilities Department is working on a project that would enable the town to receive water from its southern utilities neighbor, Orange Water and Sewer Authority. Sending Water Hillsborough can send water to: City of Durham Water Management Orange-Alamance Water System, which serves some rural areas in Orange and Alamance counties Orange Water and Sewer Authority, which serves the Carrboro and Chapel Hill area History of the Reservoir In the 1980s and early 1990s, the Hillsborough community began exploring options for addressing the town’s water shortage due to a history of droughts and water restrictions and a desire to accommodate expected future growth. In 1993, Hillsborough voters approved general obligation bonds to help pay for building the reservoir’s first phase. The first phase was built with expansion in mind. The reservoir’s 20-year permit allowed for a second phase to be started by 2018. In 2000, the reservoir was made operational earlier than scheduled and before full to help provide immediate drought relief for customers under water restrictions. Severe Droughts Hillsborough experienced severe droughts in the 1920s, 1930s, 1950s, 1980s and 2000s. In 1954, schools closed at noon and the town sought federal aid because of drought conditions. That same year, drought conditions forced the town to disconnect the water of any customer found wasting it. In 1988, mandatory water restrictions were put in place. By the early 1990s, the town completed an interconnected pipeline with the City of Durham to allow regular purchases from Durham’s water system to withstand periods of droughts and water restrictions. The town could only purchase water between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. due to demands on Durham’s system. Benefits Phase 1 of the reservoir has: Helped the town withstand several severe droughts in the 2000s. At one point, larger surrounding systems were near or below 50 days of remaining water, but Hillsborough still had enough water for 200 days. Allowed Hillsborough to accommodate new development. Many residents and businesses joining Hillsborough after 2000 would not be here today without the reservoir. The Phase 2 expansion of the reservoir: Is a long-term investment in Hillsborough’s water supply. Raised the reservoir about 10 feet, doubling its volume and providing a maximum yield of 6 million gallons of water per day. No Recreation on the Reservoir Recreation is not allowed at the West Fork Eno Reservoir or the surrounding town-owned property. This includes boating, hunting and fishing. Required Conservation Federal and state permits require a conservation easement to: Protect the town’s drinking water source. Reduce the effects of the reservoir on others. To provide a 100-foot buffer around the reservoir, the town must keep the land in a natural state with no development, recreation or access other than to maintain the reservoir. Risks The town does not have the resources to oversee public activities at the reservoir and cannot assume the risk or liability of allowing recreational activities. Recreation also could introduce invasive animals and plants. The town already funds treatment to remove a weed native to South Asia that can damage utility equipment and the environment. See the section on annual treatment for an invasive plant on this page. Seasonal Treatment for Hydrilla The state does not plan to treat the Eno River for hydrilla in 2026 due to the flooding from Tropical Storm Chantal in 2025. A survey will be conducted later this year to determine whether hydrilla treatment should resume. Typically, the state annually treats 16 miles of the Eno River with the herbicide fluridone to reduce hydrilla, an invasive aquatic plant. Applications typically start in mid-May and continue through August. The section of the river treated is below the Ben Johnston Lake dam in Orange County to Roxboro Road and U.S. 501 in Durham County. The herbicide is applied in a concentration that is safe for humans, fish and wildlife and well below limits set by the Environmental Protection Agency. Property owners next to the treated section of river should use caution in using river water for irrigation during this time. About Hydrilla Hydrilla is native to South Asia and grows rapidly, creating thick mats on the surfaces of lakes, rivers and other waterways. The weed: Negatively affects the health of fish and wildlife in the area. Can clog intakes for supplying drinking water and irrigation. Can harbor mosquitoes. Can interfere with recreation on waterways. The plant was discovered in the Eno River watershed in the early 1990s in Lake Orange, which is upstream of Hillsborough and one of the town's water sources. In 2009, biologists confirmed hydrilla in the West Fork Eno Reservoir. The town-owned reservoir is stocked with triploid grass carp to manage the invasive plant. More Information The North Carolina Division of Water Resources manages the annual treatment. Hillsborough helps fund it. For more information, contact Stormwater and Environmental Services Manager Terry Hackett by email or phone at 919-296-9621. Water Treatment Our Water Quality The town's water treatment must meet high standards set by the town, state and federal governments. Hillsborough routinely tests for more than 150 substances in the town's drinking water and meets or exceeds the standards. See the annual Water Quality Report . Water Plant Testing Staff monitor and evaluate water 24 hours a day. The plant has: A state-certified laboratory to test for bacteria daily. Two lab-certified operators who test raw and finished water at the plant every two hours — more than required by the state. Water System Testing Staff also test various points in the water system. The water system includes the pipes, pumps and tanks needed to transport and store water. Tests occur: Weekly — For bacteria at five of the farthest points in the town's water lines. Monthly — For bacteria at 15 areas. Quarterly — For disinfection byproducts. These are substances created by the process to clean water. Annually — For inorganic materials, pesticides, synthetic organic chemicals, nitrates, volatile organic compounds and secondary contaminants. Every five years — For unregulated contaminants that the Environmental Protection Agency lists for testing. Our Water Treatment Process The Hillsborough Water Treatment Plant is the processing plant for your water. The plant takes raw water from the Eno River. It then adds ingredients and applies processes to the water to make it usable. The plant focuses on: First — Cleanliness and compliance with standards. Second — Taste, odor and appearance. Water Treatment Converting raw water into drinking water includes injecting chemicals at multiple points to help remove organic material, disinfect the water and ensure longer freshness before releasing it for use by the community. The chemical process starts before the raw water reaches the Water Treatment Plant. Water released from the town's reservoir travels to Lake Ben Johnston, where the town removes water for use. At this intake location, a chemical is added to help particles in the water combine for easier removal. At the plant, more chemicals are added for the same reason and to adjust the water's color, acidity and alkalinity. Filtering Out Materials The water then goes through several filtration, aeration and clarification stages. In these stages, the water remains in large basins while being mixed at slower and slower speeds. This allows the combined large materials to drop to the bottom of the basins. Finally, the clear water moves through a fine filtration system to remove remaining particles. At this stage, the water’s turbidity is measured and filtration adjustments are made to remove any cloudiness from the water caused by large amounts of particles that are otherwise invisible to the eye. Adjusting Treatment The water is then disinfected and final adjustments to acidity and alkalinity are made before the water is pumped through pipes to homes and businesses. Throughout the treatment process, employees test the water for more than 150 contaminants, making adjustments to the treatment as needed. Hillsborough's treated wastewater is released into the Eno River. Before the water is safe to return to the river, it must go through multiple stages of treatment at the Wastewater Treatment Plant. The Eno River is within the Upper Neuse River Basin, an ecologically sensitive area. Due to this, the state imposes strict requirements on treated wastewater. Staff who maintain the pipes and pumps connected with removing your used water must be available at all hours for emergencies. The Upper Neuse River Watershed is the 770-square-mile area draining to the Falls Lake Reservoir. Our Watershed Falls Lake Rules Hillsborough is required to treat its wastewater at higher and more expensive standards than other sewer systems because it is in a watershed that drains into Falls Lake. The lake is a 12,000-acre reservoir in Durham, Granville and Wake counties. It is on the Environmental Protection Agency’s list of impaired waters and has been designated nutrient-sensitive by the North Carolina Division of Water Resources. To protect and restore the lake’s water quality, the state created the Falls Lake Rules to reduce the amount of nitrogen and phosphorous that enter Falls Lake through rivers and streams. The first stage of the wastewater discharge rules went into effect in 2016, and the second stage is expected in 2036. In 2014, Hillsborough completed upgrades to its wastewater treatment plant in part to meet the Stage 1 wastewater rule. Additional upgrades to the Wastewater Treatment Plant likely will be required to meet the Stage 2 wastewater rules. Read more about the rules from the Upper Neuse River Basin Association . Nitrogen and Phosphorus Removal Hillsborough's wastewater treatment work helps protect the Eno River, which is classified as nutrient sensitive. The town is dedicated to maintaining the high water quality of our river and has successfully reduced the total nitrogen discharged into the river by approximately 85% since 2004. In 2022, the town discharged into the Eno River only 57.6% of the allowed total nitrogen and 56.7% of the allowed total phosphorus. The allowances are provided by the Falls Lake Rules. Wastewater Treatment Our Treated Wastewater Quality The town's wastewater treatment must meet extremely high standards set by the town, state and federal governments. Hillsborough routinely tests for more than 220 substances in the town's wastewater and solids and meets or exceeds the standards. See the annual Wastewater Quality Report . Testing Staff monitor and evaluate water 24 hours a day. The plant has a laboratory to perform frequent checks on the progress of wastewater treatment. Staff also test various points in the Eno River.  Tests occur: Upstream of the water intake Before and after wastewater discharge Downstream of wastewater discharge Our Wastewater Treatment Process The plant uses an enhanced biological nutrient removal process to treat wastewater. Naturally occurring nutrients can cause algae growth, depleted oxygen, and fish kills. The nutrients — like nitrogen and phosphorus — must be brought to safe levels before treated wastewater can be discharged into the Eno River. Treatment Steps The Town of Hillsborough's wastewater treatment plant Large item removal — Bar screens remove trash, wood and rocks, which then are compacted for disposal. Grit removal — Sand and dirt are removed for disposal. Secondary treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are removed through a series of aeration tanks and sent to large tanks called digesters (see 4). The remaining wastewater moves to the clarifiers (see 5). Solids treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are treated in digesters and then thickened and trucked to a composting facility to be turned into a soil amendment. Clarification — Rakes slowly skim the wastewater surface for scum like grease, oils, plastics and soap. The scum is pumped to digesters (see 4). Solids settle and are removed for disposal. Sand filtration — The remaining water moves through 6 feet of sand, which removes additional solids. Disinfection, final treatment — Chlorine is added to kill bacteria. Chemicals are added to neutralize the chlorine. Aeration — The water is re-aerated before discharge to remove dissolved gases and to oxidize dissolved metals. Discharge — The treated wastewater is returned to the Eno River at an outfall. Wastewater Treatment Plant and Tours Wastewater Treatment Plant employees are highly certified and operate and maintain the plant to ensure compliance with state and federal permits and regulations. The plant can treat up to 3 million gallons of wastewater per day. It was built in 1977, with upgrades in 2001 and 2007 to improve solids management, nutrient removal and treatment capabilities. The most recent expansion and upgrade was completed in 2014, allowing the plant to meet state requirements to protect Falls Lake, where Hillsborough’s watershed drains. This upgrade Hillsborough’s discharged water quality among the best in the nation. Awards In previous years, the Wastewater Treatment Plant and its staff have won awards for: Professionalism in the Operation of a Wastewater Treatment Plant Solutions to Operational Problems Wastewater Treatment Plant Operations and Maintenance Wastewater Treatment Plant Operator Tours See what it takes to treat used water for return to the Eno River. Public tours are offered at 1 p.m. on the second Friday of the month in March and September. Private tours can be scheduled separately for special groups. All tours are open to a maximum of 10 people with participants at least 10 years old. All tours require a completed request form. Request a Tour Wastewater Collection and System Maintenance About Pump Stations A pump station is a collection chamber that uses pumps to lift wastewater from a lower elevation to a higher elevation, where the wastewater can flow by gravity. It pumps into a pressurized main called a force main, which ends in a sewer manhole. There, wastewater can flow by gravity to the Wastewater Treatment Plant. The pump stations require frequent maintenance and weekly inspections. Improperly disposed rags, wipes or other trash can cause expensive repairs. Failures can result in larger sanitary sewer overflows than from a gravity sewer, with subsequent fines from the state. Why Pump Stations? Hillsborough has more pump stations per customer than surrounding water and sewer systems because of the town's terrain. Also, the systems were likely preferred decades ago due to the low upfront costs. Some of the pump stations were built by developers and turned over to the town to own and operate. Blocked Sewer Lines The town assesses sewer blockages to determine the cause and location — whether they are on the utility or property owner's side of a sewer line. Customers may be responsible for the cost of investigation and repairs if their  actions cause a blockage in the town’s sewer main. Responsibilities The town owns and maintains the sewer main or sewer service line in public rights of ways or easements. It will clear blockages of lines in public rights of ways or easements. The town may require property owners to install or relocate cleanouts to the town's specifications. The town may agree to perform the work but may require reimbursement and the granting of property access from the customer. Property owners are responsible for blockages in the sewer service line between the house or structure on their property and the public right of way or easement. The town can require installation or relocation of a cleanout at the right of way or easement if one is not present. Sewer Cleanout A sewer cleanout is a capped pipe that allows access to the sewer line for maintenance and inspections. Cleanouts typically indicate the ownership line when located at the edge of the public right of way or easement. Sewer Maintenance The town’s primary responsibility for the sewer system is to protect the environment by maintaining unobstructed wastewater flow in the collection system’s main lines. Crews routinely do preventative maintenance and repairs, remove roots and clean sewer lines with pressure washers. Hillsborough's treated wastewater is released into the Eno River. Before the water is safe to return to the river, it must go through multiple stages of treatment at the Wastewater Treatment Plant. The Eno River is within the Upper Neuse River Basin, an ecologically sensitive area. Due to this, the state imposes strict requirements on treated wastewater. Staff who maintain the pipes and pumps connected with removing your used water must be available at all hours for emergencies. The Upper Neuse River Watershed is the 770-square-mile area draining to the Falls Lake Reservoir. Our Watershed Falls Lake Rules Hillsborough is required to treat its wastewater at higher and more expensive standards than other sewer systems because it is in a watershed that drains into Falls Lake. The lake is a 12,000-acre reservoir in Durham, Granville and Wake counties. It is on the Environmental Protection Agency’s list of impaired waters and has been designated nutrient-sensitive by the North Carolina Division of Water Resources. To protect and restore the lake’s water quality, the state created the Falls Lake Rules to reduce the amount of nitrogen and phosphorous that enter Falls Lake through rivers and streams. The first stage of the wastewater discharge rules went into effect in 2016, and the second stage is expected in 2036. In 2014, Hillsborough completed upgrades to its wastewater treatment plant in part to meet the Stage 1 wastewater rule. Additional upgrades to the Wastewater Treatment Plant likely will be required to meet the Stage 2 wastewater rules. Read more about the rules from the Upper Neuse River Basin Association . Nitrogen and Phosphorus Removal Hillsborough's wastewater treatment work helps protect the Eno River, which is classified as nutrient sensitive. The town is dedicated to maintaining the high water quality of our river and has successfully reduced the total nitrogen discharged into the river by approximately 85% since 2004. In 2022, the town discharged into the Eno River only 57.6% of the allowed total nitrogen and 56.7% of the allowed total phosphorus. The allowances are provided by the Falls Lake Rules. Wastewater Treatment Our Treated Wastewater Quality The town's wastewater treatment must meet extremely high standards set by the town, state and federal governments. Hillsborough routinely tests for more than 220 substances in the town's wastewater and solids and meets or exceeds the standards. See the annual Wastewater Quality Report . Testing Staff monitor and evaluate water 24 hours a day. The plant has a laboratory to perform frequent checks on the progress of wastewater treatment. Staff also test various points in the Eno River.  Tests occur: Upstream of the water intake Before and after wastewater discharge Downstream of wastewater discharge Our Wastewater Treatment Process The plant uses an enhanced biological nutrient removal process to treat wastewater. Naturally occurring nutrients can cause algae growth, depleted oxygen, and fish kills. The nutrients — like nitrogen and phosphorus — must be brought to safe levels before treated wastewater can be discharged into the Eno River. Treatment Steps The Town of Hillsborough's wastewater treatment plant Large item removal — Bar screens remove trash, wood and rocks, which then are compacted for disposal. Grit removal — Sand and dirt are removed for disposal. Secondary treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are removed through a series of aeration tanks and sent to large tanks called digesters (see 4). The remaining wastewater moves to the clarifiers (see 5). Solids treatment — Organic materials and nutrients are treated in digesters and then thickened and trucked to a composting facility to be turned into a soil amendment. Clarification — Rakes slowly skim the wastewater surface for scum like grease, oils, plastics and soap. The scum is pumped to digesters (see 4). Solids settle and are removed for disposal. Sand filtration — The remaining water moves through 6 feet of sand, which removes additional solids. Disinfection, final treatment — Chlorine is added to kill bacteria. Chemicals are added to neutralize the chlorine. Aeration — The water is re-aerated before discharge to remove dissolved gases and to oxidize dissolved metals. Discharge — The treated wastewater is returned to the Eno River at an outfall. Wastewater Treatment Plant and Tours Wastewater Treatment Plant employees are highly certified and operate and maintain the plant to ensure compliance with state and federal permits and regulations. The plant can treat up to 3 million gallons of wastewater per day. It was built in 1977, with upgrades in 2001 and 2007 to improve solids management, nutrient removal and treatment capabilities. The most recent expansion and upgrade was completed in 2014, allowing the plant to meet state requirements to protect Falls Lake, where Hillsborough’s watershed drains. This upgrade Hillsborough’s discharged water quality among the best in the nation. https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/services/: Below is information on how the town prepares for winter weather and how you can too. Many people have a Hillsborough mailing address but do not live in town limits. See the Services for Your Property page. Town Activities Preparations In advance of predicted winter weather, Hillsborough crews prepare equipment and resources, including: Outfitting trucks with plows and tire chains. Ensuring vehicles and generators are fully fueled. Ensuring any equipment that may be needed is ready to go. Pretreating some roadways with brine if needed, including Rainey Avenue; Beckett’s Ridge, Lafayette, Lakeshore, Meadowlands and Waterstone drives; East Margaret Lane; College Park Road; and Cameron Street. Operations Snow and Ice Removal Visit the Street Maintenance page to view plowing guidelines and the town's responsibilities for winter weather. Curbside Collections Hillsborough will stop curbside collections of trash, brush, bulk items and loose leaves if weather conditions prevent collection trucks from operating safely. Garbage collection will be given priority when collections resume. Orange County provides collection of recyclables. See the Orange County website for changes in its services. Parks and Trails Parks and greenways are not a priority for snow removal. When weather conditions deteriorate, staff will close parks and greenways until they determine the areas are safe. Please heed all safety signage and barricades and do not enter closed areas. Those who choose to use the town’s parks and greenways do so at their own risk. Entering closed areas or moving signs and barriers also puts others at risk and pulls emergency workers away from other duties. Community Responsibilities Preparation When weather conditions worsen, please: Stay off roads, sidewalks and town trails. Do not park vehicles on streets because this affects plowing. Do not pass vehicles plowing snow or spreading salt or brine to avoid bodily injury or damage to vehicle paint. Remember that sidewalks and roads may continue to have snow and ice and to be hazardous after a storm, particularly in shaded areas. Traveling on roads, sidewalks and trails during severe weather is risky, creates more emergency work, and slows efforts to keep roadways cleared for emergency response. Resources Emergency Information See emergency information on the Ready Hillsborough page, including key local contacts, how to report problems and how to subscribe to emergency notifications. Emergency Kits Basic readiness tips include having adequate supplies of food and water to last several days and putting together a disaster supply kit, including a flashlight, batteries, cash, first aid supplies and copies of critical documents. See the Ready Hillsborough page. Equipment and Vehicles Prepare your equipment and vehicles by ensuring they are fully fueled. Additionally, vehicles may be equipped with tire chains to improve traction and prevent slipping on snowy or icy roads. Stay Informed Please stay informed and share information with neighbors. Use the Town of Hillsborough’s various communication channels: Website — hillsboroughnc.gov News releases — Get News page to receive town news by email Facebook — @HillsboroughGov Instagram — @HillsboroughGov Nextdoor — www.nextdoor.com/pages/town-of-hillsborough-2 Bluesky — @hillsboroughnc.gov Safety Tips Low temperatures can bring power outages due to high electrical demand. Stay safe with these tips: Heater Safety If heat is out, go to a neighbor or family member’s home if possible. Do not use generators, grills, camp stoves or other gasoline or charcoal-burning devices inside the home, basement or garage or near a window. These devices create carbon monoxide gas, which is poisonous. Check heating units and carbon monoxide detectors. Poorly operating or damaged heating units can release carbon monoxide gas. Caring for Others Don't leave children, elderly people or pets alone in vehicles. Temperatures in vehicles can drop rapidly. Pets can be greatly affected by the cold and should not be exposed long. Remember that older adults, people in fragile health and small children are affected more by the cold than the average adult. Check on loved ones and neighbors, preferably by telephone. Caring for Yourself Create a warm room by sealing off the warmest room in the home where everyone gathers. Close off additional rooms, cover doorways and windows, and block drafts with towels, blankets or clothes. Avoid unnecessarily opening doors and windows. Keep body heat in by layering loose but warm clothing, wearing a hat, using blankets, and huddling with people or pets. Eat and drink regularly to help stay warm. Avoid alcohol and caffeine because they cause the body to lose heat faster. Wear appropriate clothing that will adequately insulate from the cold when outdoors. The National Weather Service advises wearing a hat and gloves if outdoors during a wind chill advisory. Avoid overexertion and be aware of the amount and intensity of physical activity indoors and outdoors. Cold weather strains the body, especially the heart. Resources Personal Safety in Extreme Cold and Power Outages — Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Fire Safety Tips — National Fire Protection Association Food Safety After Power Outages — U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Disaster Response — American Red Cross in English or Español State Road Information — 511 Information Line Pipes and Cold Weather Frozen pipes can burst and cause substantial damage and water loss. This includes fire sprinkler systems. See the Backflow Prevention page for information on protecting backflow prevention devices in winter. Preventing Frozen and Burst Pipes Use these tips to protect water pipes during freezing temperatures. Unheated Areas Pipes in unheated areas have the greatest chance of freezing. Unheated areas include attics, basements and crawl spaces. Insulate pipes ― Pipe insulation is available in fiberglass or foam sleeves. Home centers and hardware stores have sleeves providing one-eighth to five-eighths inches of insulation. Specialty dealers have products that provide up to 2 inches of insulation. The extra thickness can save a pipe. Heat pipes ― Heating cables and tapes are effective. Select a heating cable with the UL label and a built-in thermostat that turns the heat on when needed. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions closely. If you have it, turn on an incandescent light bulb in your crawl space for extra warmth. Seal openings and air leaks ― This includes access doors, air vents in the foundation, and cracks. Especially keep cold wind away from pipes, which speeds the freezing process. Close and seal cracks and other openings with insulation, cardboard, plastic or newspaper. Foundation air vents may have hinged or sliding covers to easily close the vents. Ensure your water meter box cover is closed ― The cover prevents cold air from freezing water inside the meter. If the cover is broken or missing and you are a Hillsborough water customer, call the Town of Hillsborough at 919-732-3621. Heated Areas Leave cabinet doors open under kitchen and bathroom sinks ― This allows warmer room air to circulate around pipes. Let water drip slowly from the highest faucet in the building ― Use this tip if you have difficulty protecting pipes in an unheated area or if you believe your pipes may freeze for other reasons. An open faucet allows water to escape before pressure builds to a point where a pipe can burst. If dripping stops, ice may be blocking the pipe. Keep the faucet open because the pipe still needs pressure relief. Frozen and Burst Pipes If Your Pipes Are Frozen If nothing comes out of your faucets: Leave the faucets open and call a plumber. Try to thaw the pipe with warm air from a hair dryer ― Start by warming the pipe as close to the faucet as possible. Then work toward the coldest section of pipe. Do not use electrical appliances in areas of standing water. You could be electrocuted. Do not use a torch or other open flame. This could cause a fire hazard. If Your Pipes Have Burst Turn off water at the main shutoff valve and leave faucets open ― Make sure everyone knows where the master valve is for your plumbing system and how to open and close it. The valve may be in your basement, crawl space or closet where water pipes enter the house or building. If you do not have a master shutoff valve, consider installing one. Drain the pipes in your plumbing system ― Open the highest and lowest cold-water faucets in your house until the water is depleted. Before draining pipes ― Turn off the water heater to ensure the lack of water does not burn out the heating elements. After draining pipes ― Before turning on the water heater again, ensure water service is restored and the water tank is refilled. If you fix a leak, you may qualify for an adjustment to your utility bill. See the Billing and Adjustments page.

Safety Tips Low temperatures can bring power outages due to high electrical demand. Stay safe with these tips: Heater Safety If heat is out, go to a neighbor or family member’s home if possible. Do not use generators, grills, camp stoves or other gasoline or charcoal-burning devices inside the home, basement or garage or near a window. These devices create carbon monoxide gas, which is poisonous. Check heating units and carbon monoxide detectors. Poorly operating or damaged heating units can release carbon monoxide gas. Caring for Others Don't leave children, elderly people or pets alone in vehicles. Temperatures in vehicles can drop rapidly. Pets can be greatly affected by the cold and should not be exposed long. Remember that older adults, people in fragile health and small children are affected more by the cold than the average adult. Check on loved ones and neighbors, preferably by telephone. Caring for Yourself Create a warm room by sealing off the warmest room in the home where everyone gathers. Close off additional rooms, cover doorways and windows, and block drafts with towels, blankets or clothes. Avoid unnecessarily opening doors and windows. Keep body heat in by layering loose but warm clothing, wearing a hat, using blankets, and huddling with people or pets. Eat and drink regularly to help stay warm. Avoid alcohol and caffeine because they cause the body to lose heat faster. Wear appropriate clothing that will adequately insulate from the cold when outdoors. The National Weather Service advises wearing a hat and gloves if outdoors during a wind chill advisory. Avoid overexertion and be aware of the amount and intensity of physical activity indoors and outdoors. Cold weather strains the body, especially the heart.
