Pipes and Cold Weather Frozen pipes can burst and cause substantial damage and water loss. This includes fire sprinkler systems. See the Backflow Prevention page for information on protecting backflow prevention devices in winter.

Frozen pipes can burst and cause substantial damage and water loss. This includes fire sprinkler systems. See the Backflow Prevention page for information on protecting backflow prevention devices in winter.

Preventing Frozen and Burst Pipes Use these tips to protect water pipes during freezing temperatures. Unheated Areas Pipes in unheated areas have the greatest chance of freezing. Unheated areas include attics, basements and crawl spaces. Insulate pipes ― Pipe insulation is available in fiberglass or foam sleeves. Home centers and hardware stores have sleeves providing one-eighth to five-eighths inches of insulation. Specialty dealers have products that provide up to 2 inches of insulation. The extra thickness can save a pipe. Heat pipes ― Heating cables and tapes are effective. Select a heating cable with the UL label and a built-in thermostat that turns the heat on when needed. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions closely. If you have it, turn on an incandescent light bulb in your crawl space for extra warmth. Seal openings and air leaks ― This includes access doors, air vents in the foundation, and cracks. Especially keep cold wind away from pipes, which speeds the freezing process. Close and seal cracks and other openings with insulation, cardboard, plastic or newspaper. Foundation air vents may have hinged or sliding covers to easily close the vents. Ensure your water meter box cover is closed ― The cover prevents cold air from freezing water inside the meter. If the cover is broken or missing and you are a Hillsborough water customer, call the Town of Hillsborough at 919-732-3621. Heated Areas Leave cabinet doors open under kitchen and bathroom sinks ― This allows warmer room air to circulate around pipes. Let water drip slowly from the highest faucet in the building ― Use this tip if you have difficulty protecting pipes in an unheated area or if you believe your pipes may freeze for other reasons. An open faucet allows water to escape before pressure builds to a point where a pipe can burst. If dripping stops, ice may be blocking the pipe. Keep the faucet open because the pipe still needs pressure relief. Frozen and Burst Pipes If Your Pipes Are Frozen If nothing comes out of your faucets: Leave the faucets open and call a plumber. Try to thaw the pipe with warm air from a hair dryer ― Start by warming the pipe as close to the faucet as possible. Then work toward the coldest section of pipe. Do not use electrical appliances in areas of standing water. You could be electrocuted. Do not use a torch or other open flame. This could cause a fire hazard. If Your Pipes Have Burst Turn off water at the main shutoff valve and leave faucets open ― Make sure everyone knows where the master valve is for your plumbing system and how to open and close it. The valve may be in your basement, crawl space or closet where water pipes enter the house or building. If you do not have a master shutoff valve, consider installing one. Drain the pipes in your plumbing system ― Open the highest and lowest cold-water faucets in your house until the water is depleted. Before draining pipes ― Turn off the water heater to ensure the lack of water does not burn out the heating elements. After draining pipes ― Before turning on the water heater again, ensure water service is restored and the water tank is refilled. If you fix a leak, you may qualify for an adjustment to your utility bill. See the Billing and Adjustments page.

Below is information on how the town prepares for severe storms and how you can too. Many people have a Hillsborough mailing address but do not live in town limits. See the Services for Your Property page. When it is safe to do so, crews from the town's public works division work to clear the roads of debris. Town Activities Preparations Hillsborough crews prepare equipment and resources before forecasted storms, including: Ensuring vehicles and generators are fully fueled. Ensuring any equipment that may be needed is ready to go. Clearing as many storm drains and cross pipes as possible. Operations Below is information on how the town operates during severe weather events. Curbside Collections Hillsborough will stop curbside collections of trash, brush, bulk items and loose leaves if weather conditions prevent collection trucks from operating safely. Garbage collection will be given priority when collections resume. Orange County provides collection of recyclables. See the Orange County website for changes in its services. Parks and Trails Before and during severe weather, staff will close parks and greenways as needed to keep the community and emergency workers safe. When flooding is expected, the dog park fencing at Gold Park will be placed in an open position. This prevents damage to the fencing by allowing water carrying debris to flow through the open gates. After severe weather, parks and greenways will remain closed until the town can inspect them and remove any hazards. Please heed all safety signage and barricades and do not enter closed areas. Those who choose to use the town’s parks and greenways do so at their own risk. Entering closed areas or moving signs and barriers also puts others at risk and pulls emergency workers away from other duties. Recreation in Floodplains Undeveloped floodplains often serve as public parks and recreation. The Riverwalk greenway and Gold Park were built in their locations to provide recreation in areas that otherwise would not be developed. Riverwalk was built along a sewer easement by the Eno River. It is partially located within Gold Park. Both recreation facilities were designed to withstand flooding. Community Preparation When weather conditions worsen, please stay off roads and town trails. Doing otherwise is risky and creates more emergency work. Resources Emergency Information See emergency information on the Ready Hillsborough page, including including key local contacts, how to report problems and how to subscribe to emergency notifications. Emergency Kits Basic readiness tips include having adequate supplies of food and water to last several days and putting together a disaster supply kit, including a flashlight, batteries, cash, first aid supplies and copies of critical documents. See the Ready Hillsborough page. Equipment and Vehicles Prepare your equipment and vehicles by ensuring they are fully fueled. Additionally, vehicles may be equipped with tire chains to improve traction and prevent slipping on snowy or icy roads. Stay Informed Please stay informed and share information with neighbors. News Property Owners Recognized for Outstanding Stormwater Maintenance June 23, 2026 8:00 a.m. More News The Stormwater and Environmental Services Division reduces stormwater runoff pollution from reaching local water bodies by: Complying with the town’s National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit. Regulating development practices. Educating the public about ways to reduce stormwater runoff impacts. Stormwater staff frequently make site visits to assess stormwater runoff issues in the community. Rain Barrel Program Stormwater Social Media Stormwater Fees Town Stormwater Maintenance Stormwater Permits Report Illegal Dumping into Stormwater System About Stormwater Stormwater is rainfall or snow melt that flows across surfaces into waterways. It is North Carolina’s top water-quality problem. Stormwater is not treated and often picks up pollutants as it moves across surfaces, like exposed soil, pavement and rooftops. Pollutants include: Chemicals, oil and grease Excess fertilizer and pet waste Sediment and trash The pollution can harm aquatic ecosystems and drinking water supplies. Hillsborough's drinking water comes from the Eno River. Documents Climate Impact — Rainfall intensity's effect on flooding Do You Like to Fish — Stormwater runoff pollution and its effect on fish State and Federal Regulations Hillsborough must adhere to stormwater runoff regulations from the federal and state governments. Federal Regulation Stormwater is regulated under the 1972 Federal Water Pollution Control Act, commonly called the Clean Water Act. The Environmental Protection Agency regulates discharges through the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System . Discharges include stormwater. State Regulation Within the state, the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality operates the stormwater program for the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System. Under Phase II of the rules, small municipalities that own and operate separate storm sewers must obtain a permit and  reduce stormwater pollutants from entering their systems through six minimum measures. The minimum measures for Hillsborough are: Public education and outreach on stormwater impacts. Public involvement and participation. Illicit discharge detection and elimination. Construction site stormwater runoff control (erosion control). Post-construction stormwater management for new development and redevelopment. Pollution prevention and good housekeeping for municipal operations. Local Regulations Hillsborough is required to regulate runoff within town limits. See the effect of stormwater runoff pollution on businesses in the document Don't Go Down the Drain . See the Public Infrastructure Permits page for: Construction and post-construction stormwater management requirements and applications. Information on riparian (stream) buffers and stream identification requests. Town Stormwater Plans Bellevue Branch Watershed Improvement Plan Stormwater Management Plan Illegal Dumping and Connections Report any suspected stormwater pollution or illegal dumping into the town's stormwater system. It is illegal to: Place anything other than stormwater into any part of the town’s stormwater system, including storm drains and ditches. Connect pipes to the town’s stormwater system without approval. Illegal Dumping Signs of illegal dumping: Excessive algae Floating debris Oil sheen Strong pungent or musty odor Storm pipes flowing in dry weather Surface scum or foam Unusual color or cloudiness Examples of illegal dumping: Chlorinated backwash or the draining of swimming pools Contaminated foundation drains Oil, antifreeze, chemicals, garbage, paint or cleaning fluids Sewer and septic tank discharges Untreated animal waste Wash waters from commercial and industrial activities Washing machine discharges Required Detection The town is required to find and eliminate stormwater pollution. If an illegal connection or discharge is found, the property owner will be notified. The owner could face civil penalties up to $5,000 if the issue is not corrected. Stormwater and Your Property Rights and Reasonable Use In North Carolina, common law governs stormwater runoff and drainage. Basically, a downhill property has to receive water from uphill. Water has a right to go where it wants to go ― downhill. Components of this common law: The easement of an uphill owner includes the right to accelerate and increase the natural flow of water. Natural flow means the uphill owner cannot divert or cause water to flow onto the lower land in a different manner or place than it would naturally. The downhill owner may not obstruct natural flow from above. Property owners have the legal right to make reasonable use of their property, even if development alters water flow and affects downstream owners. The uphill owner can incur liability when the change in runoff is unreasonable and causes substantial damage. Documents Stormwater Runoff Conveyances Water Flows Downhill Maintenance Responsibilities Property owners are responsible for the stormwater control measures on their private property. Owners include homeowners associations. Drainage Ditches Along Streets Property owners are required to mow drainage ditches along town streets. The town ensures water flow is not restricted in the drainage ditches along town streets. Contact the Public Works Division to request maintenance of drainage ditches. Wet and Dry Ponds Property owners are required to have  wet and dry ponds inspected annually by a private licensed inspector. The inspection report must be submitted to the Stormwater and Environmental Services Division. The third-party annual inspections may result in recommendations for maintenance or improvements. Before making a costly repair, contact town staff to check that the work is necessary. See the Ponds and Geese section if a recommendation involves addressing geese. Ponds and Geese The Stormwater and Environmental Services Division requires a 6-foot vegetated area around ponds used as stormwater control measures. In this area, non-woody vegetation must be allowed to grow to a natural height during the growing season. When this area is newly planted, Canada geese may eat or pull out the vegetation before it is fully established. Goose management can be used to ensure this vegetation is established and maintained. Once grown to a natural height, this vegetation can also help deter geese from accessing the pond. This deterrence method works best if the vegetated area is maintained consistently around the entire pond. Canada geese are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act . They are attracted to ponds, including those used as stormwater control measures. Several geese living by a pond can hurt water quality. They eat young grass shoots that help keep pollution from reaching a pond, and they drop fecal matter that can run into the water. Lack of vegetation can cause shoreline erosion, and both erosion and excessive fecal matter can lead to odor problems, algal blooms and fish kills in the pond and downstream of the pond. To improve water quality, pond management companies may suggest ways to manage Canada geese. The Stormwater and Environmental Services Division does not require property owners to deter or chase away geese. Deterring Geese Hazing Canada geese is a legal option in North Carolina for deterring geese. See more information about hazing on the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission's website. Some additional methods for deterring geese include planting tall vegetation and installing temporary or permanent fencing. Often, pond owners with the most success are those who hire a management company to help them and who use multiple methods simultaneously to deter geese. Stream Identification and Riparian Buffers The town enforces a 50-foot buffer of plantings along streams and the Eno River. Prior approval is required to clear, build or make other impacts within a stream or river buffer, also called a riparian buffer. See the Public Infrastructure Permits page for additional information and to request stream identification services. See Riparian (Stream) Buffers . About Stream and River Buffers Buffers along water bodies are undisturbed, naturally forested areas that: Provide wildlife food and habitat. Slow stormwater runoff by allowing it to soak into the ground. Buffers help protect water quality by: Controlling erosion and keeping stream banks from collapsing. Reducing flooding and pollution of waterways. Moderating stream temperature through the amount and quality of sunlight allowed on a waterbody. Woody debris in waterways also protect water quality and provide habitat for aquatic organisms. See the document Woody Debris in Streams and Rivers . Resources The division offers materials to help property owners manage stormwater and protect the environment. Contact staff to request a site visit and advice. Documents Compost Blankets Designing A Rain Garden Don't Go Down the Drain — effect of stormwater runoff pollution on businesses Lawn Care For Water Quality Stormwater Bioswales Stormwater Runoff Conveyances Water Flows Downhill Woody Debris In Streams And Rivers Websites These sites were created in partnership with Elon University students: Enhance Your Yard with Green Infrastructure — Focusing on water management that works with the natural water cycle. Climate Impact in Residential Areas — Spotlighting the effects of climate change on the local area and actions community members can take. Videos Rain Garden More Information Programs and Volunteer Opportunities Annual Herbicide Treatment Typically, the state treats the Eno River annually to reduce the invasive plant hydrilla. The town helps fund the treatment through stormwater fees. See the About Water page. Educational Programs The town partners with Orange County to provide educational programs and presentations. Topics include: Preventing stormwater pollution Maintaining stormwater ponds Other best practices Programs typically are provided for civic, school and local watershed groups, elected officials, developers, contractors and other groups interested in learning more about stormwater issues. Contact stormwater staff to request a program or presentation. Other Partnerships and Opportunities Clean Water Education Partnership — The town is a supporting member of this partnership to protect water quality in the Tar-Pamlico, Neuse and Cape Fear river basins. Hillsborough's watershed is part of the Upper Neuse River Basin. The partnership is a cooperative effort among local governments, state agencies and nonprofit organizations. It uses education and outreach to protect water quality. Eno River Association — The town partners with the association in preserving and conserving lands along the Eno River. Community members can join the association's stream monitoring program to help protect the local watershed. Volunteer Workdays — Stormwater staff offer volunteer workdays at parks, wetlands and other areas around town. Subscribe to town news releases . Publications and Reports Annual Reports Falls Lake Nutrient Sensitive Water Report — The report summarizes efforts related to new and existing developments in the previous fiscal year (July 1-June 30). It is required by the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality under the Falls Lake Stormwater Rule for New Development. Falls Lake Nutrient Sensitive Water Annual Report National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Phase II Report — The report summarizes activities of the town’s stormwater management program for the previous fiscal year (July 1-June 30). It is required under the federal Clean Water Act and state regulations. National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Phase II Annual Report Stormwater Almanac The division periodically publishes the Stormwater Almanac with news and information on the division's recent projects. Stormwater Almanac Awards Awards received by the division include: Green Infrastructure Project of the Year ― For the Odie Street bioswales project from the Stormwater Management Division of the American Public Works Association North Carolina Chapter in 2023. Contact Information Town Hall, 101 E. Orange St. 919-296-9621 Please make an appointment for in-person visits. Use the contact form or staff directory to report a stormwater pollution concern or to request an educational program. Department of Environmental Quality operates the stormwater program for the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System. Under Phase II of the rules, small municipalities that own and operate separate storm sewers must obtain a permit and  reduce stormwater pollutants from entering their systems through six minimum measures. The minimum measures for Hillsborough are: Public education and outreach on stormwater impacts. Public involvement and participation. Illicit discharge detection and elimination. Construction site stormwater runoff control (erosion control). Post-construction stormwater management for new development and redevelopment. Pollution prevention and good housekeeping for municipal operations. Local Regulations Hillsborough is required to regulate runoff within town limits. Rights and Reasonable Use In North Carolina, common law governs stormwater runoff and drainage. Basically, a downhill property has to receive water from uphill. Water has a right to go where it wants to go ― downhill. Components of this common law: The easement of an uphill owner includes the right to accelerate and increase the natural flow of water. Natural flow means the uphill owner cannot divert or cause water to flow onto the lower land in a different manner or place than it would naturally. The downhill owner may not obstruct natural flow from above. Property owners have the legal right to make reasonable use of their property, even if development alters water flow and affects downstream owners. The uphill owner can incur liability when the change in runoff is unreasonable and causes substantial damage. Owners include homeowners associations. Drainage Ditches Along Streets Property owners are required to mow drainage ditches along town streets. The town ensures water flow is not restricted in the drainage ditches along town streets. Contact the Public Works Division to request maintenance of drainage ditches. Wet and Dry Ponds Property owners are required to have  wet and dry ponds inspected annually by a private licensed inspector. The inspection report must be submitted to the Stormwater and Environmental Services Division. The third-party annual inspections may result in recommendations for maintenance or improvements. Before making a costly repair, contact town staff to check that the work is necessary. See the Ponds and Geese section if a recommendation involves addressing geese. Ponds and Geese The Stormwater and Environmental Services Division requires a 6-foot vegetated area around ponds used as stormwater control measures. In this area, non-woody vegetation must be allowed to grow to a natural height during the growing season. When this area is newly planted, Canada geese may eat or pull out the vegetation before it is fully established. Goose management can be used to ensure this vegetation is established and maintained. Once grown to a natural height, this vegetation can also help deter geese from accessing the pond. This deterrence method works best if the vegetated area is maintained consistently around the entire pond. Canada geese are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act . They are attracted to ponds, including those used as stormwater control measures. Several geese living by a pond can hurt water quality. They eat young grass shoots that help keep pollution from reaching a pond, and they drop fecal matter that can run into the water. Lack of vegetation can cause shoreline erosion, and both erosion and excessive fecal matter can lead to odor problems, algal blooms and fish kills in the pond and downstream of the pond. To improve water quality, pond management companies may suggest ways to manage Canada geese. The Stormwater and Environmental Services Division does not require property owners to deter or chase away geese. Deterring Geese Hazing Canada geese is a legal option in North Carolina for deterring geese. See more information about hazing on the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission's website. Some additional methods for deterring geese include planting tall vegetation and installing temporary or permanent fencing. Often, pond owners with the most success are those who hire a management company to help them and who use multiple methods simultaneously to deter geese. Stream Identification and Riparian Buffers The town enforces a 50-foot buffer of plantings along streams and the Eno River. Prior approval is required to clear, build or make other impacts within a stream or river buffer, also called a riparian buffer. See the Public Infrastructure Permits page for additional information and to request stream identification services. See Riparian (Stream) Buffers . About Stream and River Buffers Buffers along water bodies are undisturbed, naturally forested areas that: Provide wildlife food and habitat. Slow stormwater runoff by allowing it to soak into the ground. Buffers help protect water quality by: Controlling erosion and keeping stream banks from collapsing. Reducing flooding and pollution of waterways. Moderating stream temperature through the amount and quality of sunlight allowed on a waterbody. Woody debris in waterways also protect water quality and provide habitat for aquatic organisms. See the document Woody Debris in Streams and Rivers . Improvements are planned to the sewer system within the Lawndale Basin in northern Hillsborough. The project will involve: Cleaning and inspecting sewers. Performing small dig and repair projects on the main sewer line and on select sewer services within the right of way. Moving or installing some sewer cleanouts. Lining sewer pipes to prevent groundwater and rainwater from entering the sewer system. The town maintains a part of the sewer service line — from within the road right of way to the sewer main. A sewer cleanout is typically on the line between the property's edge and the public right of way. Site Project area The Lawndale Basin is in northern Hillsborough. The project area includes: An easement between Rainey Avenue and Torain Street. Parts of Lawndale and Rainey avenues and parts of Cornelius, Hill and Torain streets. Funding Funding The project is estimated to cost about $1.5 million. The town will receive a low-interest loan of about $1.1 million from the Clean Water State Revolving Fund, which includes loan forgiveness for up to $500,000 of the funding. The remaining part of the project will be paid for from reserve funds and should have no impact on future customer rates. Current Phase The rehabilitation and replacement project is expected to begin in November 2025. Project Details About the Project Orange County installed the sewers in this area under a grant program in the 1980s before the town assumed ownership. The sewers now need repair or replacement. A hired contractor studied the condition of the sewers and the sewer service connections from homes in the Lawndale Basin. The study included monitoring flow in the sewers during different times of day and storm events. Part of the project will involve installing a sewer cleanout pipe where one may be missing. The pipe allows access to the sewer line to remove blockages. It helps specify between public and private ownership. The town maintains the public portion of sewer lines. Property owners are responsible for the section of sewer service lines that connects to their structure from the right of way or easement. Lining a Sewer Roots and soil can enter a pipe and clog it. Cracks in the pipe also can let sewage out. Water that enters sewer pipes must be treated by the town. The blue coloring shows a relined pipe. When a sewer is relined, the service connection from a home or building is blocked temporarily. The relining process reduces disturbance to roads and yards because the work is performed by machines underground. To line a sewer: A flexible resin inverted “sock” is inserted into the sewer main through manholes. The sock is cured or hardened to the pipe's shape. Crews use hot steam or water or sometimes ultraviolet light for the curing process. A machine cuts openings in the relined pipe for any sewer services connected to the sewer main. Project Contact Julie Taylor Taylor Engineering & Consulting 336-339-6883 Contact Taylor Engineering What to Expect Sewer Service Issues When workers reline the sewer pipes: The sewer service connection from your home to the sewer line will be blocked. Pressure in the sewer line can force water out of toilets and drains. The contractor will communicate directly with residents when service disruption will occur. Service connections will be reopened at the end of the noted workday. Avoid a Sewer Backup On the day your service is disrupted: Do not do laundry, dishwashing, bathing or other activities that use large amounts of water. Keep toilets flushed after use. Place a towel on the rim of your toilet bowl and keep the seat and lid closed. Cover any basement floor drains. Odor The curing process for lining a sewer may produce an odor, like glue or a permanent marker. The odor may enter your home through the pipe that connects your home to the public sewer main. The odor is caused by styrene, a naturally occurring chemical, used in the resin of the liners. The airborne concentration levels are minimal and do not pose a health risk. During short-term exposure, the chemical can cause eye irritation, headache and discomfort. The odor will disappear once the pipe lining is fully hardened. Avoid Potential Odor To Avoid the Odor — Run water into sinks, bathtubs and drains to fill the P-trap fitting on pipes, creating a water barrier. About a gallon of water will fill the U-shaped portion of the pipe, which keeps sewer gas and other vapors out of your home or building. If Odor Is Inside — Open windows or use fans to refresh and circulate your home’s air. If Odor Remains — If the odor remains despite the steps above, contact a plumber about fixing a potential open air connection to the sewer. That problem is a health risk from sewer gas entering your home. Additional Items Timeline and Hours — The project is expected to start in November 2025. Once the project moves forward, it is expected to take about six months to complete. Construction activities will be 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday-Friday unless approved in writing by the town. Construction — Noise and traffic disruptions will occur throughout the project. Contractors may need to dig in the road or rights of way to make repairs. They will use manholes or sewer cleanouts in the right of way to reline sewers. One lane of traffic may be closed. If repairs are needed on private property, the contractor will coordinate with the resident. Markings — Workers will place paint markings or flags on the ground to identify underground utilities where digging may occur. Paint markings wash off with time. Please do not disrupt the project markings. Equipment — If equipment or materials are stored on private property, the contractor should have a written contract with the property owner. Post-construction — The contractor will restore areas disturbed by the project. Contact Information Town Hall Annex, 105 E. Corbin St. 919-296-9631 Please make an appointment for in-person visits. Contact Utilities Staff Title Phone Email Strandwitz, Marie Utilities Director 919-296-9631 Email

The town comprehensively studied its parking supply and the demand for parking in the downtown area and West Hillsborough. See current parking options.
The town comprehensively studied its parking supply and the demand for parking in the downtown area and West Hillsborough.
The study area encompasses a significant portion of the downtown area and West Hillsborough. The West Hillsborough area is a growing part of town.

Goals Effective parking strategies are essential as the town continues to invest in revitalizing its downtown area, including West Hillsborough. A strategic parking management plan will allow Hillsborough to maximize the potential of its downtown for commercial, residential and tourism growth. The proposed Ridgewalk greenway would be a paved, accessible urban greenway for pedestrians and bicyclists that connects downtown Hillsborough to the future train station site and Cates Creek Park in Waterstone. Background This project was first introduced when Collins Ridge was seeking  approval for its Master Plan. Conditions of the approval require the developers to reserve and make available to the town land to accommodate pedestrian and bicycle connectivity and to work with the town to determine the location and specific design details for pedestrian and bicycle connectivity between the parcel south of I-85 and the public rights-of-way, sidewalks, greenways, and trails in Collins Ridge. This project was identified by the Board of Commissioners as a transportation priority in September 2021. Outside Groups Coordination with the North Carolina Department of Transportation will be required as the greenway must cross Interstate 85. The current plan is for a greenway and wildlife path underneath a bridge near Collins Ridge. The town must also work with the North Carolina Railroad Company to cross the rail corridor. Location and Sections It is likely that the greenway project will be implemented in sections. The main section will be between downtown and the train station. The train station could be complete in Fiscal Year 2028, and the town plans to complete the Ridgewalk greenway connection around the same time. The second section will connect the train station to the section of greenway being built and dedicated to the town by the developers of Collins Ridge. The third section will connect Collins Ridge to Cates Creek Park. Current Phase Preliminary engineering and discussion with North Carolina Department of Transportation and the North Carolina Railroad Company have begun. More information will be provided as engineering on projects that must be finished first are completed. The town is working to replace the 1970s-era River Pumping Station, moving it from the Eno River floodplain and increasing sewer capacity in the area. Flooding during Tropical Storm Chantal in July 2025 reached the base of the fence on top of the station's concrete structure. Location and Background The River Pumping Station transports 75% of the sewage of Hillsborough's customers to the Wastewater Treatment Plant. It was built in the 1970s near the Eno River by the Wastewater Treatment Plant on Elizabeth Brady Road. The project would relocate the station to higher ground out of the Eno River's 500-year floodplain. The pumping station has a history of flooding in severe weather, including during Hurricane Fran in 1996 (right photo), a storm in 1998 (left photo), and Tropical Storm Chantal in 2025. Flooding from Tropical Storm Chantal left the station's three pumps inoperable. The town used three bypass pumps through late December 2025 to prevent sewage spills while new pumps, motors, and electrical and control systems were purchased and installed. The station was restored to service in late December. Funding The estimated cost of the project is more than $10.2 million. Grant Funding The town received a Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities grant of $5.8 million from the Federal Emergency Management Agency in August 2023. As a part of the grant, the town would pay for 30% of the project. In April 2025, the federal program was ended and all applications from fiscal years 2020-2023 were canceled. This affected Phase 2 of the River Pumping Station project, which would have used over $5.1 million in federal funds to build the new station. North Carolina and 19 other states sued FEMA in July 2025 over its decision to cancel the BRIC program. In December 2025, a U.S. district court judge ruled the program was unlawfully ended. On March 18, 2026, FEMA issued an advisory notifying states that the agency plans to resume programming support. As of June 2026, the BRIC program has been reestablished, and the town has received reimbursements from FEMA for expended design fees. The state  plans to transfer the project to its hazard mitigation grant program. Moving the project to the state's program would give the town more time to complete the project and include increased costs. Current Phase The project is  in the design phase. Had federal funding not been revoked, construction would have likely begun by the end of 2025. Staff Title Phone Email Strandwitz, Marie Utilities Director 919-296-9631 Email

South Churton Street is being studied to develop design concepts that contribute to the town's character and meet the goals of a state-funded project to widen the road from Interstate 40 to the Eno River. Funding Funding The multimodal corridor study costs $200,000. The town contributed $50,000 in Fiscal Year 2023 to match $150,000 in funding from the Metropolitan Planning Organization. Construction is currently funded by the North Carolina Department of Transportation. Schedule Schedule The planning study was completed in 2024 and endorsed by the Board of Commissioners on June 10, 2024. Project findings and recommended improvements will be shared with the North Carolina Department of Transportation to inform the future construction project. The construction project is scheduled in the draft State Transportation Improvement Program for Fiscal Year 2033. Background South Churton Street serves as the primary entrance into town from interstates 40 and 85 and is one of the more heavily traveled roads in Hillsborough. It carries between 20,000 and 25,000 annual average daily trips, many of which are generated by commuters from beyond the town limits. State Plans The State Transportation Improvement Program includes a project to widen South Churton Street from Interstate 40 to the Eno River to relieve traffic congestion and provide north-south pedestrian and bicycle connectivity. In 2019, the North Carolina Department of Transportation developed concepts for the widening project. No preferred alternative or cross section was designated by the town at that time. Town Study Town staff and leaders recognize the importance of a well-designed South Churton Street. A quality design that enhances safety, improves flow and presents a beautiful entryway to town will benefit the local community and the wider network. The town has initiated this study to develop alternatives that consider the needs of the town and all users of the corridor. The town is updating its unified development ordinance to ensure it aligns with the Hillsborough Comprehensive Sustainability Plan. The updated ordinance will set standards for quality development and land use. It will be enhanced with graphics and for ease of use. Senior Planner Tom King reviews site plans, which must meet the requirements laid out by the town's unified development ordinance. About the ordinance and project The Unified Development Ordinance contains rules that govern how land may be used and developed in town. It includes regulations related to stormwater and to zoning and land subdivision. It is guided by t he Comprehensive Sustainability Plan , which serves as Hillsborough's framework for future development and for the transition to 100% clean energy. T he current Unified Development Ordinance is available on the town's website. Rewrite As the rewrite project progresses, drafts of the ordinance will be posted to this page for public review and comment. Inspire Placemaking Collective is facilitating the update. The team of planning and urban design experts has extensive experience in providing ordinance updates to municipalities across the Southeast. Project Priorities Zoning and Land Use Keep zoning consistent with established plans Incorporate sustainability, economic resilience, and equity goals Procedures and Processes Ensure a responsive, predictable, and equitable review process Evaluate the energy efficiency of proposed developments Streamline the permitting process Housing Encourage construction of accessory dwelling units Make developments accessible and connected Promote a variety of housing types that fill the missing middle housing gap Parking Reduce surface parking Make requirements more simple and flexible Adopt electric vehicle charging requirements for developments Offer incentives to developers for electric vehicle charging infrastructure Sidewalks and Signage Update payment in lieu system to require sidewalks, crosswalks and accessible ramps Prohibit barriers to connectivity Review sidewalk dining regulations Update signage regulations Streets and Access Adopt universal design standards and complete streets policies Require developments to have bicycle and pedestrian connectivity Increase multimodal accessibility Schedule The tentative schedule below will be updated as the project continues: Project Start — April 2025 Research and Assessment — May to October 2025 Drafts, Designs and Revisions — October 2025 to May 2026 Board Review and Public Meetings — May to August 2026 Final Adoption — August 2026 Updates See the Unified Development Ordinance framework . Get Involved Engagement The project will include several opportunities for providing input, including opportunities for specific advisory groups and for the general public. Below is the planned schedule. See the town calendar for times and locations of public meetings. Technical Advisory Committee Meeting — May 2025 Partner Group Interviews — May 2025 Listening Session with Town Staff — May 2025 Informational Public Open House — June 23, 2025 Pop-up Engagement — July 24, 2025 Technical Advisory Committee Meeting — Aug. 21, 2025 Special Joint Public Meeting — Aug. 21, 2025 Public Open House — Aug. 27, 2025 Technical Advisory Committee Meetings — November 2025 to March 2026 Public Open House — May 2026 Stay Informed For regular updates: See the town's News page. Riverwalk is an urban greenway that stretches about 3 miles along the Eno River. The paved trail is accessible and travels through Gold Park and the Orange County-owned River Park. The town's trail connects to North Carolina's Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area and Historic Occoneechee Speedway Trail, a part of Eno River State Park . See the greenway's master plan for planned improvements and the Riverwalk page for more information.

Agendas and Minutes Bee City USA Treasure Trees Programs and Resources Invasive Plants Removal The invasive species removal team meets weekly to remove invasive plants from Hillsborough’s public spaces as part of a program of the Hillsborough Tree Board. The team gathers on Wednesdays for two hours in the afternoon in the cooler months and in the morning during warmer months. If it’s removal season, they bring loppers and shears to remove plants. If it’s planting season, they bring shovels and trowels. Trees Are Good The International Society of Arboriculture manages the educational website Trees Are Good, which offers quality tree care information for homeowners and other tree owners. The site helps increase awareness of the benefits of trees and provides resources to help sustain trees in an urban environment. Check out the directory to find an arborist and see the Tree Owner Resources for information, including why to hire an arborist and why topping hurts trees. Tree City USA The town has been a part of the Arbor Day Foundation's Tree City USA program since 2003. To qualify for the program, the town is required to have: A tree board or department. A tree care ordinance. A community forestry program with an annual budget of at least $2 per resident. An annual Arbor Day observance and proclamation. Programs and Resources Invasive Plants Removal The invasive species removal team meets weekly to remove invasive plants from Hillsborough’s public spaces as part of a program of the Hillsborough Tree Board. The team gathers on Wednesdays for two hours in the afternoon in the cooler months and in the morning during warmer months. If it’s removal season, they bring loppers and shears to remove plants. If it’s planting season, they bring shovels and trowels. Trees Are Good The International Society of Arboriculture manages the educational website Trees Are Good, which offers quality tree care information for homeowners and other tree owners. The site helps increase awareness of the benefits of trees and provides resources to help sustain trees in an urban environment. Check out the directory to find an arborist and see the Tree Owner Resources for information, including why to hire an arborist and why topping hurts trees. Tree City USA The town has been a part of the Arbor Day Foundation's Tree City USA program since 2003. To qualify for the program, the town is required to have: A tree board or department. A tree care ordinance. A community forestry program with an annual budget of at least $2 per resident. An annual Arbor Day observance and proclamation. https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/community: Hillsborough offers many opportunities for recreation. It does not provide recreational programming. Town-maintained parks and greenways are open daily from 7 a.m. until 30 minutes after sunset. The Public Space and Sustainability Division: Manages town parks and greenways. Implements decisions of the Parks and Recreation Board . Gold Park includes swings and other play equipment. Parks and Recreation Board Proposed Greenway Reservations Riverwalk Greenway Town Map Town Parks and Greenways See the Town Map for directions and amenities. Greenways Parks Calvin Street Greenway — This short greenway allows pedestrian and bicycle access from downtown and adjacent neighborhoods to Gold Park and Riverwalk. Riverwalk Greenway — This greenway along the Eno River connects Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area and trails east of town. See the Riverwalk page. Community Parks Cates Creek Park — 1445 Cates Creek Parkway. This community park has a pollinator garden and a skate spot . The multi-use field with soccer goals can be reserved. See the Reservations and Bee City USA pages. Gold Park — 415 Dimmocks Mill Road. This community park includes a dog park and a part of the Riverwalk greenway. The multi-use field and large picnic shelter can be reserved. See the Reservations and Bee City USA pages. See the park's trail map . Natural Area Kings Highway Park — 1001 Ben Johnston Road. This natural area with trails is surrounded in part by Lake Ben Johnston. It includes a kayak launch . Neighborhood and Pocket Parks Hillsborough Heights Park — 510 Terrell Road Mayo Park — South side of West King Street Murray Street Park — 225 Murray St. Turnip Patch Park — 333 W. King St. Dog Park The dog park is a fenced-in area in Gold Park where dogs area allowed to be off leash. It has the same hours as Gold Park. Dog Park Rules Dogs must be: At least 6 months old and not in heat. Current on all required vaccinations, with rabies tags displayed. On a maximum 6-foot leash before entering and when leaving the facility. Within sight and under voice control of owner at all times. Immediately removed if showing aggression. Owners must: Collect and dispose of all dog waste. Help keep the off-leash area safe for all visitors. Report all dog bites to Orange County Animal Control. Call 919-942-7387 or 911. Ground Covering The dog park's ground is covered with shredded hardwood mulch that: Is safe for use by children and dogs. Helps reduce dust, dirt and the ground cover’s movement. Grass has not been planted because maintenance would be difficult with the park's heavy use and because establishing grass would require several seasons of nonuse. Self-Guided Walks Interpretive Signage The town's interpretive signage helps provide context to sites within Hillsborough. The signs provide understanding of the town's history, environment and culture. Most of the signs are along the Riverwalk greenway, but there are some at other key points of interest in town. See Signage Map Treasure Trees The Treasure Trees Program recognizes the preservation of significant trees in the Hillsborough area. Trees are selected by the Tree Board. View them on the Treasure Trees page. About Our Recreation No recreation is allowed at the town's reservoir. See the About Water page. Building in Flood-Prone Areas Undeveloped floodplains often serve the need for public parks and recreation. The Riverwalk greenway and Gold Park were built in their locations to provide recreation in areas that otherwise would not be developed. These recreation facilities require cleanup after a severe weather event to remove hazards. They are open for use many more days throughout the year than they are closed for weather and maintenance. Built to Withstand Flooding Riverwalk is located partially within Gold Park and was built along a sewer easement by the Eno River. Both recreation facilities were designed to withstand flooding. Gold Park’s dog park was built with a chain-link fence to allow floodwaters through. When flooding is expected, the fencing is left open to allow water carrying debris to flow through without damaging the fence. Severe Weather Parks and greenways are closed at times for the safety of the community and emergency workers. Hazards can exist even after a storm with high winds or snow has passed or after floodwaters have receded. Parks and greenways: Will remain closed following severe weather until the town can inspect the areas and remove any hazards. Are not a priority for snow and ice removal. They will be closed in deteriorating wintry conditions until staff determines they are safe. During Closures Heed any closure signs or barriers for parks and trails. Those who choose to use the town’s parks and greenways do so at their own risk. By entering closed areas and by moving or removing closure signs and barriers, you also: Slow cleanup efforts and delay the reopening of parks and greenways for everyone. Force public works and public safety staff away from other duties to reinstall closure signs and barriers. Force emergency workers away from other duties for potential rescues. Risk the safety of others. Subscribe to town news and follow @HillsboroughGov social media to stay informed about closures and reopenings. Shade at Parks Town staff and appointed boards are working to provide shade options at parks. Fast-growing shade trees have been planted around the perimeter of Cates Creek and Gold parks. Trees are planted in available spaces around the play areas but not inside due to spacing regulations for the play equipment. Because of the play equipment's current height and spacing regulations, sunshades in the play areas would be installed at a height that would provide little sun blockage during the day and that would make the shades a safety risk in high winds. Water Fountains Water is turned off at exterior drinking fountains at parks when the first freezing temperatures of winter are forecasted. Water service then is restored in the spring when the danger of freezing temperatures has passed. This helps avoid water line breaks, which can be costly to repair and disruptive to the use of recreational areas. Make a Recommendation The Tree Board makes planting decisions for town spaces. Plants typically are added between November and March to improve survival due to less heat and more precipitation. The Parks and Recreation Board advises the town on recreation improvements and implements recommendations in recreation master plans. Other Recreation Recreation Offerings from Others Exchange Club Park is owned and maintained by the Exchange Club. Contact the club at 919-732-9283 for more information. Orange County provides recreational programming, a senior center and additional parks in and around town, including Fairview and River parks. https://www.hillsboroughnc.gov/about-us/: The town operates under a council-manager form of government. The Board of Commissioners establishes policy and law. The town manager oversees the daily operations of the town. Water Treatment Plant Superintendent Nathan Cates gives a tour of the West Fork Eno Reservoir to Government 101 participants. Board of Commissioners Government 101 Town Manager's Office Mayor and Board Roles Mayor and Board The Board of Commissioners: Makes the decisions, laws and policies for the town. Appoints a professional town manager, who serves as the board's chief adviser. The mayor: Leads and moderates Board of Commissioners meetings. Calls special meetings. Declares states of emergency for the town. Facilitates problem-solving and policy changes. Acts as the head of the town for ceremonial purposes. Town Manager Role The town manager is the town government's chief operating officer. The manager: Implements the decisions, laws and policies made by the Board of Commissioners. Coordinates the operations of town departments. Is responsible for preparing a proposed operating budget for the board. The annual budget that is adopted by the board provides funding, staffing and general guidance to town departments for the fiscal year. The fiscal year starts July 1. Town Clerk Role The state requires a clerk for each city, town and county. The town manager appoints the town clerk, who works closely with the Hillsborough Board of Commissioners. The clerk: Prepares meeting agendas. Gives legal notice of meetings. Records meeting minutes. Maintains official town records. Codifies town ordinances. Contact the clerk for public records and proclamation requests and for requests to add an item to the town board's agenda. About Commissioner Matt Hughes was appointed to the Hillsborough Board of Commissioners in 2018 and elected to his first full term in 2019. At 27 years old, he became the town’s first millennial and openly LGBTQ+ commissioner and one of its youngest commissioners ever. Hughes is a lifelong resident of Hillsborough, attending Central, Grady Brown and New Hope elementary schools and Stanback Middle and Cedar Ridge High schools. He earned a bachelor’s degree in political science and a master’s degree in public administration from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Hughes has worked in state government, higher education, politics, and nonprofits with a professional focus on policy, human resources, and finance and operations. The commissioner has served on a number of local boards and commissions, including Orange County’s board of adjustment, human relations commission and partnership for young children. He also has served as the president of the Northern Orange Branch of the NAACP and as a member of the Juvenile Justice Planning Subcommittee of the Governor's Crime Commission. Hughes is passionate about zoning reform, affordable housing, economic development and making Hillsborough a safe, affordable and enjoyable place to live, work and play.

About About Evelyn Lloyd has served as a commissioner since 1991, continuing the tradition of local service started by her father, Allen, who served 30 years on the board. She is a lifelong Hillsborough resident. Lloyd graduated from the Eshelman School of Pharmacy at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1965 and opened Lloyd’s Pharmacy in Hillsborough with her father in 1986. This downtown location allows her to hear residents’ concerns, which she faithfully shares with the board. Lloyd's family helped preserve 66 acres on Occoneechee Mountain, now designated an ecological area of national significance and protected as part of the Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area. She is a lifelong Hillsborough resident. Lloyd graduated from the Eshelman School of Pharmacy at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1965 and opened Lloyd’s Pharmacy in Hillsborough with her father in 1986. Lloyd's family helped preserve 66 acres on Occoneechee Mountain, now designated an ecological area of national significance and protected as part of the Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area. Results from the latest Community Survey show 95% of respondents rate Hillsborough as an excellent or good place to live and 89% are satisfied with the quality of services provided by the town. The town surveys community members every two years to better understand community priorities and to gather information about the quality of town programs and services. The survey allows the town to: Assess resident satisfaction with town services. Compare performance to other communities locally and nationally. Evaluate progress over time. Use the results in identifying community priorities, decision making and budgeting. Survey Results Survey Documents — 2021 Results 2023 Community Survey Executive Summary (Extracted from Findings Report) 2023 Community Survey Findings Report 2023 Community Survey GIS Maps 2023 Community Survey Open-Ended Comments Leading the Way Award The town has received the Leading the Way Award for surveys conducted in 2021 and 2023. Recipients of the award rank in the top 10% of all local governments in the United States for resident satisfaction with regard to their composite performance on ETC Institute's survey in these core areas: Overall quality of services Customer service provided by employees Value residents received for local taxes and fees. More Information The town has partnered with ETC Institute for the town's community survey since 2017. Before the award was introduced, benchmarking data provided by ETC Institute showed that Hillsborough rated significantly higher than the U.S. and regional averages for similarly sized communities in almost all of the categories. In 2020, ETC Institute created the Leading the Way Award to recognize local governments for outstanding achievement in the delivery of services to residents. The Hillsborough Police Department is always looking for individuals to join our team who have a high moral character and a genuine desire to serve and make a difference. The Town of Hillsborough is an equal opportunity employer that welcomes applicants from diverse backgrounds. All applicants will be treated in a fair and consistent manner. Selection for employment will be made based on the applicants' qualifications for the job. Opportunities may be available for: Individuals with no experience who are interested in law enforcement. Individuals looking to start a career who have completed basic law enforcement training. Lateral transfers from other agencies. Apply Police Information Recruitment Video Benefits Benefits of Joining HPD The Town of Hillsborough offers a competitive benefits package, including: Salary — The starting salary for an officer who has completed basic law enforcement training is $58,966. Hiring incentives also may be offered: 2% increase for an associate’s degree or 4% for a bachelor’s degree in a related field. Up to 3% increase for each year of comparable service, up to 25%. $1,500 for Spanish fluency. Shift differential of $4 per hour between midnight and 7 a.m. Officers may attain up to two specializations with 2.5% pay increase for each. Specializations include: Canine unit Collision investigation specialist Community engagement specialist Investigative specialist Tactical and medical specialist Traffic and drug enforcement specialist Pay scales are as follows: $58,966 to $94,345 for police officer $61,739 to $98,782 for police officer 1st class $64,679 to $103,487 for corporal Career progression — Hillsborough's two-step career progression system allows officers to advance their careers outside of regular performance evaluations and opportunities for promotion. Officers who complete certain training requirements can be eligible at 12 months of service for officer 1st class, the first step of the career progression. Each step up to corporal provides a 5% salary increase. Individually assigned vehicles — Each officer is assigned a vehicle. Officers living within 30 miles of Hillsborough may be eligible to take the vehicle home. Tuition assistance — The department prioritizes education. The town will provide up to $5,250 in tuition reimbursement each year. Training — The department also prioritizes developing and maintaining skills. Officers have an annual minimum goal of 40 hours of elective training (external training that officers choose to attend beyond their required training). Officers are allowed up to 120 hours of elective training per year. Workout time — Officers may work out for up to 1.5 hours on duty. Ask about other physical fitness incentives. Disqualifiers Disqualifiers Factors that will disqualify a candidate from joining the department include: Criminal history — Any felony or crime conviction that could have required more than two years of incarceration as punishment. Conviction of a Class B misdemeanor within the preceding five years. Conviction of multiple misdemeanor, non-traffic crimes within the preceding five years. Any history of domestic violence. A history of criminal charges that reflect poorly on the candidate’s character. Traffic violations — Having a driver's license suspended or revoked after the date of application or in the three years before. Any history of driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Multiple at-fault accidents or driving violations beyond minor speeding or right-of-way violations. Drug use — Illegal drug use beyond youthful experimentation. The department evaluates prior drug use for its extent and for how recent it was. Credit — Demonstrated history of financial irresponsibility. Other — Former military personnel discharged dishonorably and ineligible for reenlistment. Untruthfulness or intentional withholding of information from any application, interview or paperwork associated with the position. Deliberate inaccuracies or incomplete statements. Cheating on any examination or testing associated with the position. Actions or activities that call into question the candidate’s character, integrity or morality. Hiring Process Lateral Transfers and New Hire Information Police Officer candidates and non-sworn police department applicants must meet the minimum standards as required by the North Carolina Criminal Justice Standards Commission. Police Officer applicants must have completed Basic Law Enforcement Training (BLET) and be eligible for sworn status in the State of North Carolina before assuming the role of officer. Successful candidates must adhere to standards set forth in sub chapter 09B of the North Carolina Criminal Justice Employment: Education & Training. The department most frequently hires candidates who are: Completing or have completed a basic law enforcement training program. Sworn with other agencies and are seeking a change. However, the department occasionally hires and puts recruits through a basic law enforcement training program. Candidates who accept an offer to be hired as a recruit officer must agree to a two-year commitment to the Town of Hillsborough. Completing the hiring process can take several months. The process generally includes: Application — Hillsborough accepts applications through its employment website . Recruits will be required to submit all necessary documents, including: F-3 personal history statement Liability release Wri tten testing — Hillsborough uses a standardized, written, entry-level basic skills test in math, reading comprehension, grammar and incident report writing to help ensure candidates have the basic cognitive skills needed to perform the job. Physical assessment — Lateral candidates are asked to complete the Police Officer Physical Abilities Test within the state-mandated time. This requirement is waived if applicants can provide documentation that they have successfully completed the test within the past six months. Recruits will be required to complete a modified version of the Police Officer Physical Abilities Test to ensure candidates are adequately prepared to enter a basic law enforcement training program. Panel interview — Based on the results of written and physical testing, candidates will be invited to a panel interview. During this interview, three or four staff members will meet with the candidates and ask a series of questions. They will evaluate the candidates and provide a recommendation. Interview with the chief — Based on the results of the panel interview, the chief may conduct an additional interview with the candidate. This interview generally is conducted at the beginning of the process for lateral hires. Background investigation — Candidates who successfully complete the steps above will be moved as a group into the background investigation phase. The number referred varies depending on the number of openings and staff available to conduct background investigations. During the background investigation, an experienced investigator will meet with a candidate, verify all information provided and ensure no disqualifying factors or omissions exist. Conditional offer — The town will make a conditional job offer once the department is satisfied that a candidate: Has completed the hiring steps above. Is a person it wishes to hire. The conditional offer will outline salary, benefits and expectations. It is conditional upon the successful completion of some or all of the following: Drug screening Medical and psychological evaluations Polygraph testing where applicable Upon successfully completing the hiring process, a new candidate would be hired as a recruit officer and enrolled in a basic law enforcement training program at a nearby community college. The recruit officer would attend the program, and the department would provide all uniforms and materials for attending the program. Basic Law Enforcement Training We offer opportunities for interested people to enroll in and complete basic training through sponsorship or employment as a police recruit. About the Training Becoming a police officer in North Carolina requires successfully completing a basic law enforcement training program. The full-time program takes about 16-20 weeks to complete and concludes with a comprehensive written exam and skills testing. The program prepares entry-level individuals with the cognitive and physical skills needed to become certified law enforcement officers. It includes: 36 blocks of instruction with topics including: Arrest, search and seizure Driver training Firearms Motor vehicle law Practical exercises Extensive ethics training woven throughout the course. Minimum requirements to attend the basic training include being: A United States citizen. At least 20 years old. A high school graduate or having passed the General Educational Development tests. Being of good moral character. Basic law enforcement training programs are offered through many community colleges across the state. More information is available on the North Carolina Justice Academy website . Basic Training Sponsorship Individuals wishing to attended a BLET program can request that the Hillsborough Police Department sponsor them. Sponsorship allows the program’s $900 community college tuition to be waived. The individual is responsible for costs associated with books, uniforms and other supplies. Sponsorship is not an offer of employment, and neither the individual nor the agency is making a commitment. Those wishing to be considered for sponsorship must complete an application online through the town's employment website . All required documents must be submitted, including the F-3 personal history statement and the liability release. Those seeking to be considered for sponsorship must indicate this on the supplemental question that is part of the application. Sponsorship requests are considered on a case-by-case basis and generally do not involve a specific process and only minor background checks. Contact Information Police Station, 127 N. Any felony or crime conviction that could have required more than two years of incarceration as punishment.
Conviction of a Class B misdemeanor within the preceding five years.
Having a driver's license suspended or revoked after the date of application or in the three years before.
Any history of driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
Drug use — Illegal drug use beyond youthful experimentation. The department evaluates prior drug use for its extent and for how recent it was.
Former military personnel discharged dishonorably and ineligible for reenlistment.
Untruthfulness or intentional withholding of information from any application, interview or paperwork associated with the position.
Cheating on any examination or testing associated with the position.

Lateral Transfers and New Hire Information Police Officer candidates and non-sworn police department applicants must meet the minimum standards as required by the North Carolina Criminal Justice Standards Commission. Police Officer applicants must have completed Basic Law Enforcement Training (BLET) and be eligible for sworn status in the State of North Carolina before assuming the role of officer. Successful candidates must adhere to standards set forth in sub chapter 09B of the North Carolina Criminal Justice Employment: Education & Training. The department most frequently hires candidates who are: Completing or have completed a basic law enforcement training program. Sworn with other agencies and are seeking a change. However, the department occasionally hires and puts recruits through a basic law enforcement training program. Candidates who accept an offer to be hired as a recruit officer must agree to a two-year commitment to the Town of Hillsborough. Completing the hiring process can take several months. The process generally includes: Application — Hillsborough accepts applications through its employment website . Recruits will be required to submit all necessary documents, including: F-3 personal history statement Liability release Wri tten testing — Hillsborough uses a standardized, written, entry-level basic skills test in math, reading comprehension, grammar and incident report writing to help ensure candidates have the basic cognitive skills needed to perform the job. Physical assessment — Lateral candidates are asked to complete the Police Officer Physical Abilities Test within the state-mandated time. This requirement is waived if applicants can provide documentation that they have successfully completed the test within the past six months. Recruits will be required to complete a modified version of the Police Officer Physical Abilities Test to ensure candidates are adequately prepared to enter a basic law enforcement training program. Panel interview — Based on the results of written and physical testing, candidates will be invited to a panel interview. During this interview, three or four staff members will meet with the candidates and ask a series of questions. They will evaluate the candidates and provide a recommendation. Interview with the chief — Based on the results of the panel interview, the chief may conduct an additional interview with the candidate. This interview generally is conducted at the beginning of the process for lateral hires. Background investigation — Candidates who successfully complete the steps above will be moved as a group into the background investigation phase. The number referred varies depending on the number of openings and staff available to conduct background investigations. During the background investigation, an experienced investigator will meet with a candidate, verify all information provided and ensure no disqualifying factors or omissions exist. Conditional offer — The town will make a conditional job offer once the department is satisfied that a candidate: Has completed the hiring steps above. Is a person it wishes to hire. The conditional offer will outline salary, benefits and expectations. It is conditional upon the successful completion of some or all of the following: Drug screening Medical and psychological evaluations Polygraph testing where applicable Upon successfully completing the hiring process, a new candidate would be hired as a recruit officer and enrolled in a basic law enforcement training program at a nearby community college. The recruit officer would attend the program, and the department would provide all uniforms and materials for attending the program.

About the Training Becoming a police officer in North Carolina requires successfully completing a basic law enforcement training program. The full-time program takes about 16-20 weeks to complete and concludes with a comprehensive written exam and skills testing. The program prepares entry-level individuals with the cognitive and physical skills needed to become certified law enforcement officers. It includes: 36 blocks of instruction with topics including: Arrest, search and seizure Driver training Firearms Motor vehicle law Practical exercises Extensive ethics training woven throughout the course. Minimum requirements to attend the basic training include being: A United States citizen. At least 20 years old. A high school graduate or having passed the General Educational Development tests. Being of good moral character. Basic law enforcement training programs are offered through many community colleges across the state. More information is available on the North Carolina Justice Academy website . Basic Training Sponsorship Individuals wishing to attended a BLET program can request that the Hillsborough Police Department sponsor them. Sponsorship allows the program’s $900 community college tuition to be waived. The individual is responsible for costs associated with books, uniforms and other supplies. Sponsorship is not an offer of employment, and neither the individual nor the agency is making a commitment. Those wishing to be considered for sponsorship must complete an application online through the town's employment website . All required documents must be submitted, including the F-3 personal history statement and the liability release. Those seeking to be considered for sponsorship must indicate this on the supplemental question that is part of the application. Sponsorship requests are considered on a case-by-case basis and generally do not involve a specific process and only minor background checks.

Patrol officers are part of the Operations Division, which is staffed 24 hours daily. They are the most visible and accessible part of the Police Department. They serve as the front line protecting the community, responding to 911 calls for service and providing proactive high-visibility patrol. Patrol Functions Functions Patrol officers perform a wide range of patrol duties and community policing programs. In addition to responding to 911 calls for service and high-visibility patrol, they: Provide proactive traffic enforcement. Work with a social worker for services to help keep people out of the criminal justice system. In particular, they are responsible for: Apprehension of criminals and wanted persons High-visibility patrol and property checks Enforcement of motor vehicle laws Motor vehicle accidents Public and medical assistance Recovery of stolen property Community problem solving The officers also: Provide directed patrols and work with the public to deter crime. Provide field training for new officers who have completed N.C. basic law enforcement training until the officers meet standards to be certified. Patrol Tactics and Technologies Patrol Operations Officers use different tactics and technologies for patrol operations, including: Marked and unmarked vehicles. Mobile data terminals within the vehicles for access to local, state and national resources. Radar devices for conducting motor vehicle enforcement. Additionally, officers have: Basic first aid supplies in all primary patrol vehicles to assist with medical emergencies. Access to automated external defibrillators. Social Worker Services Yazmin Washington is a social worker working with the Hillsborough Police Department. The Police Department first added a social worker in October 2023  to help keep people with a history of serious mental illness from entering the criminal justice system. Yazmin Washington became the town's social worker in January 2025. She: Works with individuals both before an arrest is made and after criminal charges are brought. Provides resources and support to homeless and at-risk people. Works with trained crisis intervention officers to reduce the intensity of situations when mental health is a concern. Steps in after an event to connect individuals with services, such as transportation to doctors’ appointments and mental health counseling. Enforcement Activities Alcohol Law Enforcement The department has an alcohol law enforcement response team. The team c hecks for compliance throughout the year with: Operations that target sales to underage buyers at local businesses, including bars, restaurants and stores . Inspections of Alcohol Beverage Control permits at local businesses. Patrols dedicated to looking for impaired drivers. Traffic Enforcement Officers focus primarily on educating drivers. They place emphasize moving violations over nonmoving violations, such as those related to vehicle equipment or registration. Submit a Traffic Concern Safety Campaigns The Police Department participates in campaigns directed by the North Carolina Governor Highway Safety Program to reduce collisions, including campaigns on: Drinking and driving Seatbelts Speeding Speeding The department has digital signs for placement by roads to show drivers their current speed. One sign is moved around the town regularly. Contact Information Police Station, 127 N. Churton St. 919-296-9500 919-732-2187 (fax) Office phones are answered 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays. Call 911 for emergencies or to have an officer dispatched.
